en: Oṃ. The Gṛhyasūtra of Gautama, together with the commentary by Maskari.
Having prostrated with devotion before Vāsudeva, the primordial deity,
this compendium of all the Smṛtis is [composed] under the guise of the Gautamīya.
Today I am composing this commentary by the son of Vāmana.
What is the connection?
This is stated: there are fourteen branches of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), namely—the six auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), the four Vedas, Mīmāṃsā, and the extensive system of Logic (*nyāyavistara*).
The Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras—these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
Thus [it is said].
The connection [of the sentence] is that this *Dharmaśāstra*, which is enumerated among those [sciences], is now commenced.

Alternatively, *saṃsāra* is the continuous succession of birth, old age, and death, consisting of the conjunction with and disjunction from the body, the senses, and their objects, for the sake of a person’s experience of pleasure and pain;
and that [succession] has its cause in *dharma* and *adharma*, and not in any other cause.
Since these two, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), are the causes for the experience of the desirable and the undesirable, they are objects to be either adopted or avoided.
Since neither of these is possible without thorough knowledge, Gautama composed this treatise for the purpose of understanding the true nature of merit and demerit;
indeed, this is its very purpose.
This is because the adoption of dharma and the avoidance of adharma constitute the purpose of human existence.
The subject matter [of this work] consists of the *aṣṭakā* rites and so forth;
just as the *agniṣṭoma* and other sacrifices prescribed by the Vedas must necessarily be performed, so too must the *aṣṭakā* rites and others.
In this regard, since it is observed that all effects proceed from causes, he first states the following in order to establish the specific nature of the cause:
"The Veda is the root of Dharma. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.1)
Now, since the scripture consists of injunctions and prohibitions, one should have stated only such things as "the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa is in the eighth [year]," and so forth;
it should not have been stated that "the Veda is the root of dharma," and so on, because that is merely a restatement (anuvāda).

Because a restatement is devoid of purpose; nor is the authority of the Veda established by this [restatement], since that is established intrinsically (*svataḥ*). Otherwise, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), wherein the authority of that which establishes the authority [of the Veda] would be established by another, and that by yet another.
It is said: this is a restatement of the fact that the Veda is the root of Dharma, intended to establish that Smṛti and conduct (śīla) are also rooted in Dharma by means of it.

If one asks how so, it is explained: from the utterance of a Vedic statement, there arises for those who know the meaning of its words an indubitable comprehension of a specific matter, which remains unchanged across different times, places, persons, and circumstances.
Or rather, that which is free from error is the root of Dharma;
and when a cognition arises that is both free from doubt and non-erroneous, its validity can be determined.
Furthermore, the falsity of a cognition produced by the Veda cannot be attributed to defects in its causes.
Because an agent is not admitted;
for it is a defect residing in the agent that brings about the falsity of the cognition produced by the word.
Thus, this is a restatement for the sake of what follows.
Now the Sūtra is being explained: therein, the Veda is the collection of texts known as Mantra and Brāhmaṇa.
[The root] *vid* means "to know"; it is called the Veda because by means of it the nature of Dharma and other such matters is known.
Although the Smṛtis and other sources possess a similarity to this, [they are distinct].
Nevertheless, there is no fault, because [the term] is used in its conventional sense (*rūḍha*), as in the case of terms like *parivrājaka*.
Accordingly, another Smṛti states:
"The Śruti is to be understood as the Veda, while the Dharmaśāstra is indeed the Smṛti."
Thus it is said.
And that [dharma] is divided according to the distinctions of the Ṛgveda and so forth;
the singular number is used with reference to its genus.
"Dharma" means action or conduct; this is the meaning.
Or it is called "the unprecedented" (apūrva).
It is the root, the cause, the indicator; that is to say, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

If it is argued that the Veda, consisting of injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), alone functions as the means for understanding *dharma* and so forth, and not that which takes the form of mantras and explanatory passages (*arthavāda*), we reply: since even the explanatory passages and the like assist by forming a single syntactical unit with the injunctions, it is not contradictory for them to be an indirect source of *dharma*. To begin with, the explanatory passage attains the nature of an injunction or prohibition by way of praise or censure.
But the mantra, because it serves to remind one of the enjoined matter at the time of performance, [is also a source].
Therefore, the Veda in its entirety is the root of Dharma.

Some maintain that [the authority of the Smṛtis] is rooted solely in *mantra* and *arthavāda*, as in the case of the passage "O traveler, you are like a watering-place in the desert," where it is concluded that a watering-place must be constructed,
and so forth. Others, however, say that the accomplishment of dharma arises from the mere study [of the Veda], as it has been said:
Truly, that twice-born man performs the highest austerity even unto his fingertips who, though wearing a garland, studies his own sacred texts daily to the best of his ability.
Thus it is said.
Therefore, [the claim] that the Vedic text alone is the root of Dharma is incorrect;
for it would entail the consequence of rendering the scriptural teachings on the fruits of action purposeless.
Furthermore, because the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the fruit of Vedic study is not a transcendental reality (apūrva);
or else, the action expressed by the Veda is denoted by the word "Veda," and that [action] is the root of Dharma.

If it is argued that [this] does not apply to the hawk-sacrifice and similar rites, it is said in reply: even there, through the protection of one's life, wealth, children, wife, and so forth by means of slaying an enemy, dharma certainly exists.
From this it is understood that whatever is seen here—such as children, cattle, villages, and the like—and whatever...
Whatever unseen force (adṛṣṭa) exists at the beginning of creation,
all of that has dharma as its cause.

Dharma is of five kinds: the dharma of caste (*varṇadharma*), the dharma of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*), the dharma of qualities (*guṇadharma*), the dharma of both caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*), and the dharma of specific occasions (*nimittadharma*).

The dharma of caste consists of study and so forth; the dharma of the stages of life consists of the placing of fuel on the sacred fire and so forth; the dharma of qualities consists of the protection and other duties of one endowed with qualities such as consecration (*abhiṣeka*).

The dharma of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) consists of such rules as "the staff of a Brāhmaṇa shall be made of *pālāśa* wood," and so forth; the dharma pertaining to specific occasions (*nimittadharma*) consists of penances (*prāyaścitta*) and the like.
"Root" (*mūla*) means the cause.
And so it has been said: "For Dharma indeed shone forth from the Veda.
Furthermore, the purpose for commencing this Sūtra is to show that just as the Veda is the root of Dharma, so too are Smṛti and Śīla.
The Veda alone is not the sole root of dharma; what then?
It is also the tradition and conduct of those who know it. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.2)

And those [two], namely tradition (smṛti) and conduct (śīla), which belong to the knowers of the Veda, are also rooted in dharma; they too must not contradict the Veda, because the text begins with the phrase "of those who know that" (tadvidām).
Furthermore, since the word "root" (mūla) is connected with both [tradition and conduct], it should be understood as having a dual ending.
By the word "that" (tat), the Veda with its six limbs is indicated.

Smṛti is that which is based upon [the Veda] and was composed by Manu, Yama, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Bṛhaspati, Uśanas, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, Āpastamba, Saṃvarta, Vyāsa, Śātātapa, Śaṅkha, Likhita, Hārīta, Bodhāyana, Yājñavalkya, Pracetas, and others.
Conduct not bound by [the rules of] morality refers to customs such as auspicious rites and ceremonies; it is "not bound" because of its great variety and because it differs according to each region.
The word "and" (ca) serves to include what has not been explicitly mentioned.
As Manu said:
The entire Veda is the root of Dharma, as are the Smṛtis and the conduct of those who know it,
as well as the practice of the virtuous and the self-satisfaction of one's own soul.
Thus [it is said].

Performing three circumambulations and so forth at the time of concluding the twilight prayers is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*). That conviction which arises from those who know the Vedas and are devoted to the performance of all duties, being free from fault, is "satisfaction of the self" (*ātmatuṣṭi*).
He will say: "And that which the wise and aged... and so forth.

Some describe [the matter] as follows: just like the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites, there is no formal injunction for these auspicious ceremonies (*kautuka-maṅgala*) and the like, because there is no transgression (*pratyavāya*) in their non-performance.
Furthermore, both "custom" (*ācāra*) and "self-satisfaction" (*ātmatuṣṭi*) are already included within "virtue" (*śīla*), and thus they are not mentioned separately.
The word "and" (*ca*) also serves merely to include what has been previously stated.
Now, the opponent raises an objection: the conduct of those who know the Veda is not the root of Dharma, because a transgression of Dharma is observed [among them]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.3)
The ellipsis is "it does not attain the status of being rooted in Dharma.
For example, as Prajāpati lusted after his own daughter;
as Indra’s approach to Ahalyā and so forth; and as Vyāsa, Bhīṣma, and others remained outside the stages of life (āśrama).
Moreover:
"And the transgression of the great is grave. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.4)

In this case as well, the implication is that it does not attain the status of being rooted in dharma (*dharmamūlatva*), because of the inclusion of the word "and" (*ca*). By the word *saha*, strength (*bala*) is meant;
as Nārada says: "Strength is what is called *saha* here."
Therefore, that which is done without regard for the treatises and worldly convention is recklessness (*sāhasa*).
This refers to those who are great and renowned in the world;
for example, Rāma’s slaying of women such as Tāṭakā.
The severing of the head of Jamadagnya’s mother,
the drowning of Vasiṣṭha in water, and so forth—
therefore, it is incorrect that moral conduct is the root of dharma.
Furthermore, what is the distinction between the transgression of dharma and rashness? That which is practiced improperly out of desire for sense objects is the transgression of dharma;
that which is done under the sway of anger and so forth is rashness.
To this, he states the following reply:
"But not so when the object is perceptible, because of the weakness of inference. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.5)
The word "tu" (but) serves to exclude the alternative position.
That which has a visible purpose—that is, a visible motive—in such a case where there is a visible motive, ethical discipline (*śīla*) is not the root of the Dharma.
And thus:
Vasiṣṭha states: "Dharma is that whose cause is not perceived.
This is not a definition;
rather, it refers to the transgression of dharma and acts of violence committed for a visible purpose.
When that [word] is being grasped, since the designation *pragṛhya* applies by the rule "īd-ud-e-t-" etc., the reading "dṛṣṭārthe avaradaurbalyāt" would result.

The meaning of "from the weakness of the inferior" (*avaradaurbalyāt*) is as follows: "inferior" (*avara*) means not superior (*na vara*), i.e., base, overcome by hatred and so forth, one who lacks knowledge of the ultimate reality; "from his weakness" means from his incapacity for the full discernment of dharma and adharma.
And by this, it is made known that even among the great who possess such knowledge, there is sometimes an overcoming [by passion].
Because pleasure and pain are inevitable for those who possess a body,
therefore, as long as they are overwhelmed by defects such as passion and the like, their conduct is not to be accepted.
And so says Vasiṣṭha: "But the cultured man (śiṣṭa) is one whose nature is free from desire. Alternatively, by the word *avara* (inferior), the men of the present Kali age are meant;
[the practice is not for them] because of their weakness and lack of capacity.

Having thus stated the authority of tradition (smṛti), he now says—addressing the question of what should be done when there is a mutual contradiction between sentences that apply to the same subject matter:
"When there is a conflict between [authorities] of equal strength, there is an option. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.6)
An object established by an equal means of valid cognition possesses equal force;
when there is mutual contradiction between these two, it should be understood that there is an option, expressed as "either this or that."
There is no abandonment of both,
because both are established by valid means of cognition;
nor is there the acceptance of only one.
"If one [alternative] were adopted, there would be the consequence of the other being rendered meaningless.

What is the illustration? First, with regard to the revealed scripture (*śruti*), there are such [injunctions] as: "The oblation should be offered after sunrise," and "The oblation should be offered before sunrise," and so forth.

In the *Smṛti* as well, Gautama states: "That which is constantly defiled by hair or insects is unfit to be eaten. Furthermore: "Food that has been pecked at by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon, sneezed over, or defiled by hair and insects is purified by the scattering of earth."
Thus says Manu.
Now, one might object: since the alternative (vikalpa) is established here by implication alone, this sūtra is redundant; for a conjunction (samuccaya) is simply not possible here.

Indeed, it is not possible to offer after the sun has risen once again after having offered before its rising, because it is improper for the principal act—the oblation—to be repeated on account of a subordinate factor such as time.
For the qualities (guṇas) are subject to the control of primordial matter (pradhāna), but primordial matter is not subject to the control of the qualities;
moreover, it is impossible for both to be the cause at the same time.
In the same way, even regarding mindfulness (*smṛti*), a combination [of both] through the abandonment of purity is not possible,
because they are mutually contradictory;
nor is the abandonment of both appropriate, as has already been stated.
Therefore, in this case, only conceptual construction results; thus, there is no purpose served by this [statement].
In that case, this is a restatement of what is established by logic for the sake of specifying a particular point.
What is the distinction? It is that when two [contradictory rules] possess equal force, there is an option (*vikalpa*); however, when they possess unequal force, there is only sublation (*bādha*).
Therefore, when there is a conflict between Śruti and Smṛti, the Smṛti alone is sublated;
for in the case of Śruti, the word is directly perceived, whereas in the case of Smṛti, it is inferential.
And an inference does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts direct perception.
Thus, when there is a conflict between Smṛti and custom (ācāra), customs such as marrying the daughter of one's maternal uncle are set aside;
for in that case, Smṛti is inferred from custom.
This is because, in the event of a conflict, an option (vikalpa) is prescribed.
But when there is no contradiction, there is a combination of those things enjoined by equal authorities, as in the case of sipping water (ācamana) and other such acts during Vedic rituals.

Now, if it is argued that the unequal strength of Smṛti with respect to Śruti is established precisely by the admission that Smṛti originates from the indicative marks (liṅga) of the Veda, then in the case of those indicative marks found in Mantras and Arthavādas— which, though directed toward other matters, serve as the basis for Smārta duties, such as “the boys like unbared swords” (kumārā viśikhā iva)— when these conflict with an explicit Vedic statement, they would be contradicted by the inference of a conflicting Vedic sentence.

[Otherwise] weakness would follow [for the Smṛti]. But when it is accepted that a Smṛti is preceded by lost Vedic branches—as Āpastamba has said: "The injunctions declared in the Brāhmaṇas have their recensions lost; they are inferred from practice"—then, since both are Vedic in origin, it follows that they possess exactly equal authority.
For there is no difference in strength between an inferred Vedic statement and a directly perceived one, just as in the case of fire determined through perception and inference.
It might be argued that where a Smṛti statement contradicts the Veda, it cannot be the basis for inferring a Vedic text;
rather, it must arise from error or some other such cause.
And that is not tenable;
for if one were to admit that the author of the *Dharmaśāstra* is untrustworthy, it would follow that there could be no confidence [in his work].

Even when the *Smṛti* is accepted as having come down through an uninterrupted tradition like the Veda, its status as being of equal authority remains untenable; thus, in that case as well, it is simply not justified.

As for that custom which was proposed, such as marrying the daughter of one’s maternal uncle and so forth, it does not qualify as the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*) because it is a corrupt practice occurring when one is overcome by desire and other passions.

However, that which is practiced without contradiction by the learned who possess the aforementioned characteristics, being equally rooted in the Veda, necessarily attains equal authority with the Smṛti.
Furthermore, a different purpose has been taught for those practices that have a basis and those that lack a basis.

Furthermore, the relative strength or weakness of traditional practice (*samācāra*)—based on its form being mediated by other Smṛti statements—is not established through the proximity of an inference of a Vedic statement.
To this it is replied: first of all, the inequality of strength among the Vedas and the other sources is understood precisely from the force (*sāmarthya*) of the commencement of this Sūtra itself.

For if these were of equal strength, then in the event of a conflict, an option (*vikalpa*) would be established by that very force; what then would be the purpose of this Sūtra? Furthermore, the mention of "equal strength" (*tulyabala*) would be rendered meaningless.
In this case as well, the greater strength of the Smṛti based on the Veda and so forth is established;
it has been stated that its origin from an indicative mark (liṅga) is thus justified.
Therefore, this alone [is the conclusion].
A position that is logically sound is called an independent position (*vastu-svatantra-pakṣa*);
yet such a position is extremely difficult to establish when [the rule] "and the tradition and conduct of those who know it" is taken as the basis.
Therefore, it is most faultlessly established that the Smṛtis originate solely from the indicative marks (liṅga) of the Veda.

But even so, this is not tenable, because in some cases we observe that Śruti is sublated by Smṛti; for example, while the entitlement to perform Vedic rites applies generally, it is restricted by Smṛti to specific individuals such as those who have undergone initiation (upanīta).
Likewise, when there is a connection with a quality of the self through even a single part of the purificatory rite (saṃskāra), a specific fruit is declared [to result].
Likewise, although the slaughter of a cow is enjoined by the Vedic injunction "one should sacrifice a cow," it is not performed because the prohibition found in the Smṛti is more authoritative.

Similarly, rites such as the Agnihotra, which are enjoined as means of livelihood and accomplished through material substances, are not performed by acquiring those substances even through theft and the like—which are prohibited by the Smṛti.
Therefore, the claim that the Smṛti is sublated by the Śruti is incorrect.
It is said: the consideration of the relative strength and weakness of means of knowledge is appropriate only when there is a conflict;
however, where no conflict exists, even that which is weak is not sublated at all.
Thus, the eligibility for ritual action belonging to one who has been initiated is not in any way contradicted by the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*).
Since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) has the purpose of acquiring the Veda, and that [acquisition] has the purpose of performing ritual acts,
the accomplishment of the primary rite cannot occur without a connection to an unseen potency (*apūrva*).

As for what was said—that even though enjoined by the Śruti, the *govardheya* sacrifice is not performed—that too is not based on Smṛti alone, but also from the wording of the Mantra: "Do not let the cows perish; let the horses perish," and so forth.
Therefore, Śruti is never sublated by Smṛti.
Some say that Smṛti is preceded by a lost branch [of the Veda];
that is incorrect.
In this regard, it is investigated: were the branches lost prior to the recollection, or at a later time?
If they were lost prior [to the recollection], then recollection would not be possible there, because they have already perished.
Because memory resembles its prior cognition,
if it were to occur at a later time,
it would not be appropriate to say that it is preceded by an extinct branch [of the Veda].
This is because they are being perceived at that time.

This is also the intended meaning of what was stated by Āpastamba: "They have perished in some places, but not everywhere. An explanation must also be provided for the statement: "Their lost readings are inferred from usage."
Thus, this definition of the means of knowing Dharma has been stated. Now, in order to state that which is measured by memory (smṛti), he says:
"The initiation of a Brāhmaṇa [should take place] in the eighth [year]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.7)
*Upanayana* is the leading near [the child] to the Veda, to the fire, to the teacher, or to the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*).
That occurs in the eighth year,
because of the conventional usage regarding the counting of years.

This time for initiation is perpetual (*nitya*), because it is stated to follow after [the prescribed times] for optional (*kāmya*) and emergency (*āpaddharma*) initiations; and because it is stated to follow after those for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya. As for the Śūdra, since he possesses only one caste (*ekajāti*), the mention of the Brāhmaṇa—though its meaning is already established—is undertaken for the purpose of establishing that [the term "Brāhmaṇa"] has "caste" as its cause.
Furthermore, Brahminhood is not something produced [by ritual] like the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*).
And thus, injunctions made with reference to a Brahmin— such as "They should pour hot [liquor] upon the Brahmin who drinks *surā*"— apply even to one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*).
Alternatively, if the mention of the "Brāhmaṇa" were omitted, this [rite] would be obligatory for all three [classes];
however, as an optional rite, it would pertain to the Brāhmaṇa in the ninth or fifth year,
while for the other two, it would occur in the eleventh and twelfth years respectively.

Because it is mentioned immediately after the optional rites (*kāmya*), one is entitled [to the subsequent rites] through initiation (*upanayana*) even when prior sacraments (*saṃskāra*) have occurred; however, without this [initiation], one is not entitled to the subsequent ones. Thus, without mentioning the rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), the commencement here is specifically that of initiation.
The optional [sacrifice] is performed on the ninth or the fifth day.
"Kāmya" means beneficial for desire—that which is capable of producing it.

Although one should have stated "in the fifth or the ninth," the deviation from the sequence is intended to include the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas in the period for optional marriage between these two [the third and fourth months].
And so says Manu:
For a king seeking military power, it is on the sixth day; for a Vaiśya seeking wealth, it is on the eighth.
The mention of "odd months" is for the purpose of indicating the distinction between optional rites (*kāmya*);
thus another *smṛti* states: "In the ninth [month] for one desiring long life; in the fifth for one desiring Vedic splendor (*brahmavarcasa*). The word "or" (*vā*) signifies an option.
He is to be seen according to one's wish.
The number of years begins from conception. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.9)
The ten months associated with the embryo are called "the womb" (garbha);
the calculation of years should begin from that point, and not from birth.
And consequently, in such passages as "the initiation of a Brāhmaṇa," the phrase "in the eighth year from conception" and so forth should be applied.
That is his second birth. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.10)
That initiation ceremony (upanayana) is the second birth; the meaning is that one who has been consecrated by it becomes a twice-born (dvija). [As stated: "Study is for the twice-born."
In such passages as these, the designation "twice-born" (dvija) is employed for the sake of conventional usage;
its inclusion is intended to encompass both the obligatory and the optional initiatory rites (upanayana).
For that reason, he is the teacher (ācārya). (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.11)
The inclusion of the term "that" (tat) is for the purpose of including both the obligatory and optional initiations (*upanayana*);
the designation is made for the sake of conventional usage in such passages as, "The teacher (*ācārya*) is the best among gurus."
And because of the recitation of the Vedas. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.12)
"Vedānuvacanaṃ" means the recitation of the entire Veda.
It is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*) that the teacher [performs it] by teaching even a single portion.
And so says Manu:
One should know that person as a teacher in this world by virtue of that service of learning, whoever benefits one with their learning, whether it be little or much.
Thus [it is said].
If the purpose has been seen, he is an *upādhyāya*;

thus Vasiṣṭha says: "But he who [teaches] one part is an *upādhyāya*. By the use of the word "and" (*ca*), it is also implied that one who explains the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) is likewise [an *upādhyāya*].
And thus Yāska says: "An *ācārya* gathers (*ācinoti*) conducts, he gathers meanings, or he gathers [wisdom] through the intellect."
Some explain the word "ca" (and) in the preceding sūtra as having the sense of conjunction;
therefore, the Teacher [Ācārya] is so called precisely because he performs both functions.
And thus says Manu:
But that twice-born man who, having initiated a pupil, teaches him the Veda along with the Kalpas and the secret doctrines (Upanishads), him they call an Ācārya.
Thus it is said.
For the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, [the periods are] eleven and twelve [years], respectively. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.13)
This time is eternal,
because it is mentioned after the sections on optional rites and those performed for specific purposes.
But when there should be an omission of either the obligatory or the optional rites due to some cause such as famine, he then states the rule for times of distress:
"The *sāvitrī* [initiation] of a Brāhmaṇa does not lapse until the sixteenth year. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.14)
The prefix *ā-* has the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*),
as in "together with the sixteenth year," meaning "of [a period] exceeding two [years]."
This is because of this indicative mark (*liṅga*), and also because another Smṛti text is seen stating, "In the sixteenth year, [one may eat] whatever one desires.
"Not fallen" means not having lost [their status].
By the word "Sāvitrī," its means—initiation (upanayana)—is intended; the meaning is that one becomes eligible for initiation.
And thus, even if the father and others have not been initiated, one is made eligible for initiation through penance.
And likewise Āpastamba says: "He whose father... grandfather... great-grandfather... and so forth.
For a Rājanya, there are two shares. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.15)
Here too, the particle *āṅ* (inclusive) continues to apply, as does the requirement of being accompanied by the age of sixteen.
The use of the term *rājanya* is for the purpose of establishing his status as a king;
thus, only one who has been initiated (*upanīta*) is entitled to the kingship.
For a Vaiśya, it is two years more. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.16)
That which consists of twenty-two together with two additional [units] is "dvyadhikā," meaning "of twenty-four.

Although it should have been stated as "caturviṃśateḥ" (of twenty-four), this specific expression is used in order to indicate that the prefix *aṅ* [in the preceding rule] signifies inclusion (*abhividhi*).
The time for initiation has been stated.
Now, with the desire to describe its requirements, he says:
"The girdles are made of muñja grass, a bowstring, or hempen thread, respectively. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.17)
The *mauñjī* is a product of *muñja* grass;
*mūrvā* is well known,
and the *maurvī* is a product of that.
The term *jyā* and *maurvī* form a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇasamāsa*). Consequently, it should be taken after removing it from the bow. *Sūtra* refers to a hemp-cord.
The bowstring has one strand,
while the others have three;
as Manu says:
The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of muñja grass, triple-stranded, even, and smooth;
that of a Kṣatriya, however, should be a bowstring made of mūrvā fiber; and that of a Vaiśya, a cord woven from hemp fibers.
Thus it is said.
The mention of "succession" (*krama*) is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of two [types of] bowstrings (*jyā* or *maurvī*).
Some describe it as being optional (*vaikalpika*) in the case of their absence.
And so says Manu:
In the absence of muñja grass, however, [the girdle] should be made from kuśa, aśmantaka, or balbaja;
it should have three strands and one, three, or five knots.
Because, since the sequence is established by logic, the mention of it serves another purpose.
The skins of the black antelope, the spotted deer, and the goat.
The word *ajina* (hide) is connected with each [term].
*Kṛṣṇa* refers to the black antelope;
*ruru* refers to the spotted deer.
*Bastaḥ* means well-known.
These are, respectively, the upper garments.
And so it is stated in another Smṛti: "They should wear only the deerskin as an upper garment."
The garments for all are made of hemp, linen, bark, and blankets.
The section on *śāṇa*: *śāṇa* [is so called].
*Kṣumā* is *atasī* (linseed); its derivative product is *kṣauma* (linen).
Cīra is made from darbha grass and similar materials;
kutapa is made from the wool of mountain-dwelling goats;
these are lower garments.

Since it is already established that all [the items] apply because of their odd number, the mention of "all" in the other Smṛti— "A garment of hemp or linen for a Brāhmaṇa"— is intended either to prevent a one-to-one correspondence (*yathāsaṅkhya*) with that specific rule, or to indicate that [the rule] applies to all [castes].
And cotton that has not been processed. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.20)
The words "of all" and "clothing" carry over from the previous context.
"Unaltered" means it is not connected with passion;
the meaning is that it is naturally white.
And the word "ca" (and) is intended to indicate that the preceding [qualities] are also unmodified.
Some [say] even the saffron robe [is not to be worn]. (Gautama 1.21)
Some also maintain that there is a connection with passion;
the word "also" (api) is used for the sake of censure.
Therefore, it should be understood as referring to the absence of the aforementioned [causes].
Now, for the sake of providing a restriction regarding the side of the ochre robe, he says:
"For a Brāhmaṇa, [the staff] is made of wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.22)
Or a garment made from tree bark processed with the decoction of vṛṣaka is the dress of a Brāhmaṇa.
Māñjiṣṭha and hāridra [dyes] are for the other two [classes]. 1.23.
That which is dyed with madder is for a Kṣatriya;
that which is dyed with turmeric is for a Vaiśya.
The staffs of a Brāhmaṇa are made of *bailva* or *pālāśa* wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.24)
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made of Bilva or Palāśa wood;
even though they are mentioned in a copulative compound, it is nevertheless stated that "or [wood] fit for sacrifice for all."
Because of the use of the singular number in this [text],
and because of the observation of another Smṛti stating, "having taken the desired staff," it is proper that only one [staff] be carried.
In the remaining cases, [the ladles] are made of *aśvattha* or *pīlu* wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.25)
The *aśvattha* is well-known;
the *pīlu* is *kalki*;
in the remaining cases, it refers to the *kṣatriya* and *vaiśya*.
In that case as well, the sacrificial post for a Kṣatriya is made of Aśvattha wood,
and for a Vaiśya, of Pīlu wood.
Or rather, all [of these] are fit for sacrifice. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.26)
Or it may be a specific type of tree suitable for sacrifice, meaning one that is free from the *vibhītaka*, *bilvaka*, *yāvaka*, and so forth;
the word "or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative in the absence [of the former],
and thus refers to its absence in the case of the preceding [options].
Otherwise, the word "or" (vā) would be meaningless; [the inclusion of] "all" is intended so that it may not apply only to the two immediately preceding [cases].
Now he states the qualities of the staff: "It should be unblemished, curved like a sacrificial post, and possessed of bark. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.27)
"Unoppressed" means not damaged by things such as vines, insects that wrap around them, fire, and so forth.
"Curved like a sacrificial post" (yūpavakra) means having tips bent like a sacrificial post. "With bark" (saśalka) means possessing their outer skin.
All of these are of such a nature without being compounded,
and not according to their respective order.
Thus Manu said:
All of them should be straight, without blemishes, and pleasant to behold;
they should not cause alarm to people, possess their bark intact, and be undamaged by fire.
Thus.
They are respectively the size of the head, the forehead, and the tip of the nose. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.28)
The word "measure" (pramāṇa) is connected with each [term]:
the height of a Brahmin is measured to the top of the head, while that of a Kṣatriya is measured to the forehead.
The nose-tip measure is for the Vaiśya;
and so Manu says:
The staff of a Brāhmaṇa should be made according to the measurement reaching to the hairline;
that of a king should reach the forehead, and that of a Vaiśya should reach the nose.
Thus [it is said].
Now he describes the dress of the religious student (brahmacārin):
"Those with shaven heads, those with matted hair, and those with tufts of matted hair. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.29)
A *muṇḍa* is one whose head is shaven;
a *jaṭila* is one who has hair;
one for whom the topknot itself is a matted lock is a *śikhājaṭa*.

Thus, by the word "muṇḍa," the act of complete tonsure is expressed. The particle *vā* has the sense of "or" and is connected with each term individually—as "either shaven-headed, or matted-haired, or with a topknot of matted hair.
The plural number is used with reference to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas.
Or rather, it was not stated [in that way] for the purpose of precluding the sequential order.
And so Manu says:
"He may be shaven-headed, or he may have matted hair, or he may have a single lock of matted hair on the crown."
Thus it is said.
Now, since the qualification for study depends upon purity, the purification of objects is first stated for the sake of purity:
"One who has something in hand while being impure from food remnants should set it down and perform the sipping of water (ācamana). (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.30)
When one who has been engaged in activities such as feeding Brahmins, holding a substance in hand and previously not impure, becomes impure through contact with something impure for some reason,
he should then place that substance on the ground and perform *ācamana*.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha:
While serving food, if he should touch something that is impure by contact with remnants,
he should set that object down on the ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and then serve again.
Thus.
If the intention were to describe the purification of the person, the mention of "taking the object with the hand" would be purposeless;
therefore, purification of the object occurs merely by setting it down, while that of the person occurs through sipping water (ācamana).

As for the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of an object mentioned in another Smṛti— "An object becomes pure by being placed on the ground and then sprinkled"— that should be understood as referring specifically to edible cooked substances.
But how is a distinction to be understood from a rule formulated with identical wording— that one should rinse after placing [the vessel] down, but not when not placing it down?
It is said: if not placing [the object] were intended, then one would have to say only this much—"one who has something in hand and is impure should sip water";
what, then, would be accomplished by the act of placing?
Therefore, it is understood that because it exceeds the requirements of the Sūtra, the position of depositing [the object] is indeed intended.
As for that which was stated by Manu: "But if one whose hand holds an object is somehow touched by something defiled..."
Without setting that object down, one who has sipped water attains purity.
Thus [it is said].
This should be understood as referring to substances that are not fit for consumption.
Thus, in the case of edible substances such as unripe plantains and the like, purification occurs merely by setting them aside;
whereas in the case of those that have been cooked, purification occurs by placing them on the ground and sprinkling water over them.
For substances that cannot be consumed, such as clothing and the like, purification is achieved by not placing them down and then sipping water.
Now he states the purification of substances:
"The purification of substances made of metal, clay, wood, and woven cloth consists of wiping, burning, scraping, and washing. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.31)
The purification of substances such as those made of metal is achieved through methods such as scrubbing, performed in their proper sequence.
Once their status as substances is established, the specific mention of them as "substances" is for the purpose of indicating their capacity to accomplish their own respective functions;
consequently, broken vessels and the like do not undergo purification.
Those things which are made from fire as their material cause are "fiery" (taijasa), such as gold and the like.
Regarding those fiery objects that are smeared with food leavings:
why is this so? Because for objects defiled by urine and the like, other rules for purification are prescribed in another Smṛti.

Likewise, the *Uśanasa-smṛti* states: "For metallic objects defiled by urine, feces, semen, or a corpse, there shall be scrubbing, scraping, and wiping twenty-one times with ashes; for non-metallic objects defiled in this manner, there shall be discarding. Similarly, regarding an object defiled by the impurities of another body, the *Kaṇva-smṛti* begins: "For objects defiled by phlegm and the like, purification is achieved by wiping twenty-one times."

Accordingly, the statement of Auśanas regarding those defiled by the untouchable (aspṛśya) or by food-leavings (ucchiṣṭa) is appropriately introduced: "For those defiled by an Anuloma Śūdra, a dog, or a crow, there is scraping; for those among the Pratilomas defiled by the touchable, there is wiping twenty-one times; for those defiled by the untouchable, there is overturning.

Likewise, the statement of Śaṅkha regarding those defiled by meat or blood is introduced: "Substances for purification include earth, brick, the paste of iṅguda, bilva, and mustard seeds, cow's urine, cow dung, and so forth."

Likewise, there is the statement of Paiṭhīnasi: "In the case of vessels defiled by a menstruating woman or other impurities, purification occurs by immersing them in pañcagavya for one day and scrubbing them twenty-one times.
Similarly, other methods of purification for metallic objects defiled by various types of impurities are prescribed in other Smṛti texts as well.
Therefore, it is proper to prescribe [purification] only for those things smeared with food-remnants.
For those items smeared with remnants, the wiping is to be done all around, on every side, with ash.
This applies to earthenware—that is, objects made of clay—when they have been defiled by contact with the untouchable.

Why? Because a specific distinction is seen in another Smṛti. Likewise, there is the statement of Uśanas: "For earthen vessels smeared with food-leavings, there is wiping; for those touched by leavings, there is sprinkling.
Similarly, there is the statement of Vasiṣṭha:
An earthen vessel that has been touched by liquor, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears,
or blood cannot be purified even by baking it again.
Thus, the abandonment of items defiled by liquor and the like has been stated;
however, in this context, it is more reasonable to assume that this refers specifically to those items contaminated by *caṇḍālas* and others.
"Pradāha" means burning thoroughly—that is, the restoration of the original state.

For wooden items such as seats, beds, and the like, which have been defiled by impurities and so forth, there is the requirement of planing or thinning them down to the extent that they were affected.
For those touched by the untouchable, there is sprinkling (prokṣaṇa). Why? Because it is said: "Sprinkling is for solid objects."
Thus, according to the statement of Manu:
"The washing of those things that can be washed by washing [is prescribed] for woven items—
that is, those made of threads such as cotton and other such products— when they have been defiled by contact with the untouchable."
Regarding purification when defiled by impurities, another Smṛti text should be consulted: "Washing, cutting off that much [of the garment], or discarding [it].
This refers to Paiṭhīnasi’s statement: "[This applies] to clothes and other items defiled by impurities and the like."

Likewise, one should observe those [rules] stated by Manu, such as "with *śrīphala* fruits for silken cloths" (*aṃśupaṭṭānām*) and so forth; and for many garments defiled by untouchables, there is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), as in the rule: "for many grains and garments."
Since Manu has thus prescribed purification by sprinkling alone, therefore,
for small quantities defiled by those who are untouchable, there is cleansing by washing.
[The perception of] metals, crystals, gems, conch-shells, and mother-of-pearl [is like that of fire]. (Gautama Sūtra 1.32)
The purification of stones and the like is like that of metallic objects;
this extension [of the rule] is for the purpose of referring to the purification mentioned in other Smṛtis.
Regarding stones and gems, it is indeed heard [in scripture]:
An unblemished golden vessel is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver that have not been otherwise treated.
And for conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and gems, purification is by means of cow's urine or water.
Thus says the word of Manu;
"by milk [the purification] of conch-shells and mother-of-pearl," thus says the word of Paiṭhīnasi.
In the case of bone and earth, [the purification is] like that for wood. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.33)
Bone refers to substances fit for common use, such as elephant tusks and the like.

By stating that "land, houses, and so forth are like wood"—thereby applying an extension (*atideśa*) based on the material substance—he makes this known: that whatever impurity is declared for a modification (*vikāra*), that very same impurity applies to the material substance (*prakṛtidravya*) as well. Otherwise, he would have had to say they are "like wooden objects."
The extension [of the rule] regarding bones and the ground has the purpose of referring to what is taught in another Smṛti;
and likewise, the extension has the purpose of referring to what is taught in another Smṛti.
And so says another Smṛti: "Bones and ground that have been touched by those who are untouchable are purified by sprinkling."
Thus spoke Kaṇva.
And the sowing of the earth. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.34)
The mention of "ground" (*bhūmi*) is for the purpose of excluding bones.
From the *Cakora*, other [details] mentioned in other Smṛtis should also be understood.
Thus it has been stated by Vasiṣṭha:
The earth is purified by four means: by digging, by burning, by trampling by cows, and also by smearing; and by a fifth, by plastering.
Thus it is said;
and likewise Manu states:
"By sweeping, by sprinkling, by burning, and by scraping..."
And by the dwelling of cows, the ground becomes pure through five [methods].
Thus,
purification should be performed according to the nature of the stain, either by means of an alternative option or by their combination.
[The purification] of cotton, bark-fiber, split bamboo, and leather [is by sprinkling]. // Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.35 //
A rope is made from *darbha* grass and the like;

a wicker-work (*vidala*) is made from bamboo, peacock feathers, and so forth; and leather refers to tiger skins and the like. When these are touched by those who are untouchable, their purification is like that of cloth—that is, like that of garments.
By the word "leather" (*carman*), which denotes the raw material, its derivatives are also included.

There is an extension of the rule even to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of ropes and the like for the purpose of their re-entry [into use]. Therefore, even the sprinkling of those things touched by the untouchable (*aspṛśya*) must be performed.
And so Paiṭhīnasi says: "The purification of ropes, mats of split bamboo, and skins when touched by the untouchable is achieved through sprinkling."
Or there is the discarding of those that are utterly defiled.
Or there may be the relinquishing of [objects] such as ropes;
this is a conventional distinction.
Therefore, there is the relinquishing of those that are utterly impaired.
The purification for others is as follows.

Now, since it has been stated that "one who has something in hand or is impure from eating should rinse the mouth after setting it down," he speaks with the intention of prescribing that rite of rinsing:
"One should begin the act of purification facing either the east or the north. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.37)
"Facing east or north" is an option according to one's preference.
But is not the mention of "purity" (śauca) redundant, since he will state later, "having sipped water" (ācamya)?
"Because the purpose is accomplished by that alone," it is said:
"Other auxiliary elements of purification as well—one should perform them facing precisely that direction.
And thus, one should also perform the washing of the feet and so forth facing that very same direction.
"One should begin" means for the sake of concentration;
therefore, one should remain with an undistracted mind for as long as it takes to complete the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Seated in a clean place, having placed his right arm between his knees, wearing the sacrificial cord over the left shoulder, having washed his hands up to the wrists, and remaining silent, he should sip water three or four times so that it touches his heart. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.38) "In a clean place" means in a spot that is not defiled;
and in this way, the washing of the feet is also established by implication, lest it be omitted.
Because of its connection with the parts of the body that are impure, the location (the ground) also becomes impure;
and thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Having washed both feet and the hands up to the wrists.
One should remain seated, not in any other posture.
And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "One should not sip water while walking, standing, lying down, or bowing.
Having placed the right arm between the knees, [he should wear] the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta).
Even if one should happen to remain seated without the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*), one must nevertheless necessarily wear it during the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Thus Āpastamba says: "One should wear the sacrificial thread while attending upon teachers, elders, guests, performing oblations (*homa*), reciting prayers (*japa*), eating, sipping water, and studying the Veda.
This is either because the thread is an integral part of the *ācamana* rite, or for the purpose of producing another sacrificial thread specifically for that occasion.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "For Snātakas, there should always be an inner garment as well as an upper one;
two sacred threads, a staff, and a water-pot with water."
Thus it is said.
The wrist-joint (*maṇibandha*) is that place where a jewel (*maṇi*) is bound;
having washed the hands from that wrist-joint upwards, one should, with speech restrained and silently, touch the heart—that is, let the water reach the heart.
This is for the purpose of defining the quantity of water.
They should be of such a quantity as to submerge a masha-bean;
thus Uśanas says: "They should reach the heart, being of the measure that submerges a masha-bean.
Regarding the options of "three times" or "four times," the choice is determined by the verse: "May the waters purify... [and so forth].
Having recited the mantra beginning with these words, one performs the sipping of water (ācamana); in that case, it is done four times, whereas elsewhere it is three times.

The explicit mention of "water" (ap) is for the purpose of excluding cow-urine and the like; otherwise, because they share the common quality of being causes of purification, there might be a misconception that they should also be used.
Or [it is for] the purpose of avoiding warm water, bubbles, foam, astringent decoctions, and so forth.
While one could simply say "he should drink" (*pibet*), the use of the longer term "he should sip" (*ācāmet*) in the aphorism is intended to include other specific rules.

In this regard, Uśanas says: "Having placed the palm of the right hand in the shape of a cow's ear, he should drink silently through the *brāhma* tīrtha, meditating upon the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas."
One should wipe [the mouth] twice. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.39)
The lips are as they are naturally formed,
because this has not been specifically stated here and because of the observation of other Smṛtis.
It is by means of the *brāhma* *tīrtha* alone.
The prefix *pari-* is used for the purpose of including other specific methods.
Regarding this, Kaṇva has stated: "Meditating upon the Atharvaveda, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas, one should wipe the region of the hair on the lips by means of the *brāhma* *tīrtha*."
And he should sprinkle water on his feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.40)
By the use of the word "ca" (and), the mouth is also included.
The prefix "abhi" is for the purpose of including other alternative rules.
Regarding this, Bhārgava says: "Then one should wipe the lips and the mouth."
He should wipe himself while meditating on Agni; then he should sprinkle his feet while meditating on Viṣṇu.
And he should touch the apertures of the head. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.41)
The apertures in the head are the eyes, nose, and ears;
by the word "and" (ca), the heart is also included.
And so Manu says:
One should first sip water three times, then wipe the mouth twice;
one should touch the cavities with water, as well as oneself, the heart, and the head.
Thus.

The prefix *upa* is for the purpose of including other methods. Therefore, having meditated on the eyes as the moon and the sun while touching [the face] with the thumb and the ring finger, and having touched [thereafter], one should meditate on the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in the nostrils while touching [them] with the index finger and the thumb;
then, having touched [thereafter], one should meditate on the quarters of space in the ears while touching [them] with the little finger and the thumb; and then [touch] with the thumb.
"One should touch the heart with the *kevala* [mantra], meditating upon the Self."
And one should place [the water] upon the head. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.42)
If it were to be stated [only] "on the head," the inclusion of the word "should place" (dadyāt) would be for the purpose of including all the fingers;
thus another Smṛti says: "Having meditated on Śrī with all the fingers, one should cast [the water] upon the head.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), [it is implied] also on the left hand.
And likewise Vasiṣṭha says: "And one should place [water] on the head and on the left hand.

Since no specific rule is stated for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, this same procedure for sipping (ācamana) applies to them as well. Furthermore, because another Smṛti states, "Women and Śūdras [should do it] once each," it should be understood that for women and Śūdras, purification is achieved by drinking water once and touching the lips once, even though this is not explicitly mentioned here.
Acamana is not required solely upon touching what has been left over from a meal;
he now states other occasions for acamana:
"After sleeping, after eating, and after sneezing. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.43)

The repetition [of the word "again"] is for the purpose of indicating that one should perform the sipping of water (ācamana) both at the beginning and at the end; the particle "ca" (and) implies also after bathing and after weeping.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having slept, having eaten, having sneezed, having bathed, having drunk, and having wept, one who has already sipped water should sip water again."

If it is argued that because the time of hunger is uncertain, sipping water (ācamana) is impossible at the very outset, [we reply that] even in that case, the undertaking is for the sake of constant purity.
As Āpastamba has said: "Even for a moment, one should not remain impure when capable [of being pure].
This is because, following sleep and other such states, sipping water is required for one who was previously pure, by the force of the initial undertaking.

Therefore, one should perform *ācamana* (sipping water) both at the beginning and at the end of that meal; regarding this, some desire that one should perform *ācamana* twice even at the very beginning.
Thus says Āpastamba: "One who is about to eat, being pure, should sip water twice.
Others, however, desire that there be *ācamana* twice only at the end of sleeping and other such acts, as Hośanā states:

"Having slept, eaten, sneezed, bathed, drunk, or wept, one who has sipped water (ācānta) should sip water again twice. Thus, the established conclusion is that there are two sippings of water at the beginning and end of a meal; one at the beginning and two at the end after sleeping and so forth; and for one who has sneezed, because it is not fixed [as to when it occurs], there are two only at the end.
Now, since impurity would result from contact with food remnants, he says:
"In the case of particles stuck to the teeth, they are treated like the teeth themselves, except when touched by the tongue."
The meaning is that when parts of food— whether solid or soft— are stuck between the teeth, one does not become impure by leavings,
provided they are not touched by the tongue.
Regarding this as well, some say: "Until the fall [from the stage]. (Gautama Sūtra 1.44)
Some maintain that even when there is contact with the tongue, as long as they do not fall from their place, they remain pure.
One should know that when insects have fallen [into food], it is as with the outflows; one becomes pure by swallowing it as if it were already consumed.
Just as water that has fallen into the mouth from an impure source becomes pure upon being swallowed,
so too there is no suspicion of needing to perform an ablution (ācamana); this is the meaning.
In this way, even while swallowing saliva, one remains pure;
for why should it be said that one is pure when swallowing what has fallen [from the teeth], given that the rule begins with "one should know [it] to be like saliva"?
Gautama, however, maintains that if there is contact with the tongue of what is stuck between the teeth, one becomes impure.
"But according to another opinion, [it is] prior to death.
This is a settled alternative:
for one authorized to perform ritual acts, there is sipping of water (ācamana), but not for anyone else.

Just as a particle of food residue that has fallen outside renders one impure, so too would it follow for a drop of sweat; therefore, he says: "Minute droplets do not render one impure when they do not fall upon the body. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.47)

The term *mukhya* refers to those minute particles (*vipruṣ*) or droplets originating in the mouth; these do not cause a loss of ritual purity (*aprāyatya*) when they issue forth from one who is reciting mantras, provided they do not fall upon a limb such as the breast or the belly.
The word *ni* signifies certainty; therefore, it is certain that only if they actually fall upon a limb do they render one impure by making one *ucchiṣṭa*, and not by mere suspicion.
Thus, a particle of what has been left over (*ucchiṣṭāvayava*), falling anywhere, causes one to become *ucchiṣṭa*.
The established tenet is that the outflow is indeed a limb [of dependent origination].
Now this is stated for the sake of all forms of purification: "Purification consists in the removal of stains and odors from that which is smeared with impure substances. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.48)
When the removal of stains and odors has been performed, that which was smeared with impurity or connected with impurity becomes pure;
by the word "impurity," the twelve types of impurities (mala) are meant.
As Manu said: "Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, nasal mucus, earwax, excrement, phlegm, tears, and rheum from the eyes— these twelve are the impurities of human beings."
The mention of "smearing" (*lepa*) is because phlegm and other such substances, though their odors are not manifest, are seen merely as smears.
The mention of "odor" (*gandha*) is because urine and other such substances are not perceived as smears, but their odor alone is perceived.

Furthermore, the repetition of the word "purity" (*śauca*) in the context of purification is for the purpose of indicating that even metallic objects and the like attain purity solely through the removal of both smears and odors.
To the question "By what means should that be done?", he says:
"That [purification] is first by water, and also by earth. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.49)
That purification is first with water, then with clay;
by the use of the word "and" (ca), it is understood that it is then performed with both.
The mention of "that" (tat) is for the purpose of including the removal of food residues as well by means of powder and so forth.

Although it could have been stated simply as "with that [water] and with clay," the inclusion of the word "preceding" (pūrva) is for the purpose of indicating that where no significant residue is observed, purification is by water alone;
as Manu says:
"A golden vessel, being free of residue, is purified by water alone."
One made of lotus-fiber, one made of stone, and likewise one made of silver that is unadorned.
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, this is for the purpose of establishing that wherever purification is prescribed, purification must first be performed with water alone.
Just as [water] is combined with clay—as in the expression "with clay and water"—so too is this non-compound construction intended to include ashes and other substances.
Since substances such as *taijasa* (metallic) have already been mentioned, this purification should be understood to apply to a limb of the body smeared with impure matter.
And in the case of contact with urine, feces, semen, exudations, or food. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.50)
The word "ca" (and) serves to draw in the act of sipping water (*ācamana*).
"Visraṃsana" means casting away;
this is connected individually with urine, feces, and oily secretions.
The connection with food refers to the consumption of edible substances.
Because that [food] is impure, the prescription for sipping water (*ācamana*) is stated for the purpose of removing stains and odors, as in the rule:
"after sleeping and after eating."
Since this has been established by the preceding [text], one should remove the smearings and odors by washing with earth and water.

And thus, regarding what was stated in the verse "first with water" (*tadadbhiḥ pūrvam*)— namely, the removal of food-smearings by means of powder and so forth— it should be understood that this [removal by washing] is impossible [to achieve by those means].
Alternatively, even the mention of the connection with eating is intended solely for the purpose of rinsing the mouth;
it is restated— though already established by the phrase "having slept or having eaten"— for the sake of indicating the proper sequence.

How is it that by the mention of "that" (tad), the removal of food-smeared [particles] is intended? It is for the purpose of indicating that one should first remove those [smeared particles] and then sip water (ācamana); otherwise, there would be doubt.

Thus says Āpastamba: "Having voided urine or feces, having washed away the smears of urine and feces, the smears of food, the smears of leavings, and whatever smears of semen there may be, and having washed his feet and sipped water, he becomes pure."
Urine and feces are well known.
"Sneha" (viscous matter) refers to semen.

The mention of urine and the other substances is for the purpose of [prescribing] sipping water (*ācamana*); as for the removal of stains and odors, it is governed by the rule: "Purification consists in the removal of stains and odors."
Because it is already established by this very [statement].
And where the sacred tradition (āmnāya) may enjoin [a practice]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.51)
In that context, "that very thing" remains, this being the remainder [of the sentence].
"Āmnāya" means the Veda;
where, in the matter of sacrifice, it would prescribe purification by mere washing of the wooden sword (sphya) and other implements, there "that very thing" [applies].
The act of carving and so forth does not [apply] by virtue of the commonality of being wood.

If it is argued that this is established precisely because their strengths are unequal, [the reply is: this is stated for the purpose of preventing what is enjoined by the Veda from entering into the worldly domain;
just as, in the context of sacrifice, purification is declared by the Veda to be through washing with water.
Even though she is occupied with worldly tasks,
this mention is made so that, by means of the commonality of the ladle, she might not perform what is prescribed in the Śruti, but rather what is prescribed in the Smṛti.
Alternatively, by the word "Āmnāya," Manu is meant.
Wherever one should perform purification, that very rule applies there, as in "for ascetics, however, it is fourfold," and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no doubt because this has already been stated, we reply: in a matter where nothing is specifically mentioned, that which is stated in another Smṛti applies.

Wherever something such as the removal of stains or odors is mentioned, a doubt arises regarding an alternative option based on another Smṛti; therefore, to exclude that, it is stated: "And where the Veda may enjoin [it].
Thus, even when the removal of stains and odors has been performed, one must still rely on such rules as, "For a student of sacred knowledge, it is double."
Now, he states the rule for approaching the teacher for the purpose of study by a student who has performed the purification:
"Having grasped the left hand [of the teacher] except for the thumb, he should address the teacher, saying: 'Recite, sir! (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.52).
Having grasped with his right hand the left hand of the teacher—the instructor—with the exception of the thumb, he should request the teacher, saying, "Recite, sir!
The mention of the hand is for the purpose of excluding the feet;
and because the context concerns the hand, it is understood that "the left" refers specifically to the left hand.
It is understood that the grasping occurs at the region of the fingers, because it has been stated that the thumb is not to be used.
Furthermore, in that regard, the eye is the mind. (Gautama Sūtra 1.53)
The meaning is that one should fix the eyes and the mind upon the guru there.
Furthermore:
the touching of the vital breaths [the mouth and nostrils] with *darbha* grass. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.54)
The word "kāryam" (should be done) is understood as the ellipsis.
Since it is impossible to directly touch the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the term "prāṇa" here refers to the sense organs located in the head, such as the eyes and so forth.
One should touch them with *darbha* grass according to the sequence prescribed for the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*).
Furthermore:
"The three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) consist of fifteen measures (mātrās). (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.55)
The word "should be performed" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Prāṇāyāma is the restraint of the vital breath, remaining without exhalation;
these three should be performed.
Each consists of exactly fifteen *mātrās*.
A *mātrā* is what is commonly known in the world by the expression "the snap of a thumb and middle finger."
Furthermore:
"And the seat should have its grass blades pointing eastward. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.56)
On seats made of darbha grass with their tips pointing eastward— this being understood from the context— he should sit down.
The word "kāryam" (should be performed) is to be understood as the ellipsis; and by the word "ca" (and), the *darbha* strainer and the living being are also included.
Furthermore:
"The five *vyāhṛtis*, preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *satya*. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.57)
The word "should be cited" is the ellipsis.
Each [of these] begins with the *praṇava* (OM), consists of the three worlds starting with *bhūr*, has *puruṣa* in the middle, and ends with *satya*;
thus it is well known in the Jābāli Śruti.
Furthermore:
"In the morning, there is the clasping of the feet of the teacher. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.58)
The word "kāryam" (should be done) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Although one might have said "upasaṅgrahaṇam" (clasping), the use of the term "pāda" (feet) is for the purpose of including the rules taught in other Smṛtis.
As Manu says:
The clasping of the teacher's feet should be performed with crossed hands:
the left foot is to be touched with the left hand, and the right foot with the right hand.
Thus it is said.
Having risen day after day at dawn,
one should perform the ritual touching of the vital breaths for oneself before the formal salutation to the Guru, so that the Guru does not have to do it for himself.
Furthermore:
"And at the beginning and end of the recitation of the Veda, [one should offer water to Brahman]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.59)
"At the beginning and end of the Vedic recitation" means at its commencement and conclusion;
the word "ca" (and) serves to include the clasping of the feet.
Furthermore:
Having been permitted, he should sit facing east; the disciple should sit to his right, facing either north or east. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.60)

Instructed by the teacher, he should sit to the south of him, facing either east or north; the option depends on what is possible. The meaning is that he should sit facing either east or north in such a way that he is directed toward the teacher while the teacher is seated. How so? "There, with a fourfold mind."
Because it has been stated thus;
the mention of "the pupil" is for the purpose of making known that this same rule applies to anyone else who has approached [for instruction].
"Permitted, [he sits] to the south."
And this is for the purpose of restriction: one should not sit down without being invited, nor on the right side.
Furthermore:
"And the Sāvitrī is to be recited at the beginning when undertaking the Veda. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.61)
The Sāvitrī begins with "tat savituḥ" and so forth; by the use of the word "and" (ca), the Vyāhṛtis preceded by the syllable Oṃ are also included.
And thus says Manu:
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable *oṃ*,
together with the three-footed *gāyatrī*, should be known as the mouth of Brahman.
Thus it is said.
The *anuvacana* (recitation) is to be studied. "In the taking up of the *brahman*" means at the commencement of the Veda; that is to say, at the time of beginning the study.
"From the beginning" means previously.
Furthermore:
"The syllable *oṃ* [is used] elsewhere as well. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.62)
Immediately after the recitation, the syllable *oṃ* should also be uttered; this applies elsewhere as well.
Herein is the sequence: having risen in the morning, one should perform the clasping of the teacher's feet;
then, being summoned by him, one should sit upon *darbha* grass.
Then, there is the touching of the vital breaths with *darbha* grass;
then, having performed breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and recited the five *mahāvyāhṛtis*, [he says] with joined palms, "Recite, sir! (*adhīhi bhoḥ*).
Having thus addressed the teacher,
and having recited the Vyāhṛtis preceded by the syllable *oṃ* as well as the Sāvitrī, he should study with the *praṇava* at the beginning.
Why is this rule restricted to the very first lesson?
Although one should say that he should then study the *Sāvitrī* and the *Anuvacana*, the text begins with "from the first taking up of the Veda" (*ādito brahmaṇa ādāne*).
Having uttered only the syllable *Oṃ* every day, why? Because it has been stated elsewhere that "the syllable *Oṃ* [is used] in other cases."
"Except for the first chapter" means elsewhere;
the word "also" (api) indicates that even in the first chapter, the syllable *praṇava* is to be inserted.
Some, by the phrase "even elsewhere," maintain that the *praṇava* should be used at the beginning of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) and so forth.
Furthermore, if he goes between [the teacher and his wife], there must be a renewed initiation. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.63)

If someone should pass between those who are studying, then for the sake of expiation, one must again perform the entire procedure beginning with the clasping of the feet and ending with the utterance of the *praṇava*.
Even though this is not part of the formal context (*aprakaraṇe*), the expiation is prescribed so that the study may be performed immediately thereafter. This applies to the passing of human beings.
Because the others are mentioned subsequently,
and because no prohibition of study (*anadhyāya*) is heard here, one should study immediately after the penance. The mention again [of the rule] refers to the first undertaking of study.

Because there is no approaching [of a teacher] in other cases, therefore, in other instances, one must perform the approaching solely for the purpose of expiation; immediately after that, the study must be performed.
Thus said Āpastamba: "Having said, 'Recite, sir,' one should either study or teach."
Furthermore:
for dogs, mongooses, snakes, frogs, and cats, there shall be a fast of three days and staying away from home. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.64)
These are well-known [cases].

For each of the [animals] beginning with the dog, the penance is the abandonment of food for three days during the interval; "separation from a Brahmin" (vipravāsa) means staying for one day separated from one's teacher.

And thus, from the very instruction regarding separation from one's teacher, the accomplishment of a one-day suspension of study (*anadhyāya*) follows. If it is asked, "How is the attainment of the one-day period established?", it is because of the irregularity of the compound. Otherwise, [the author] would have stated, "three days of fasting and staying away."
Therefore, there is non-study for only one day.
And so Manu says:
"In the case of [the death of] a cow, a frog, a cat, a dog, a snake, or a mongoose..."
One should know that there is no study during the interval of travel, whether by day or by night.
Thus [it is said].

Thus, here too, the mention of the dog is an indicative term (*upalakṣaṇa*) for four-footed animals (*catuṣpada-paśu*), since the cat is included within the category of four-footed animals. The separate mention of the cat, however, is for the purpose of prescribing a more severe penance (*prāyaścitta-gaurava*).
As Uśanas says: "Upon intercourse with a cat, one should consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and fast for three days."
The particle "ca" (and) serves to draw in the act of approaching [the teacher].
Therefore, having performed that [approaching] at the time of study, one should study.
Some say that fasting and the abandonment of study [are required].
Whether that is logical or illogical must be investigated.
Furthermore:
"For others, there are breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and the consumption of clarified butter."—Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.65.
For others, such as crows and the like, there are three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*),
because of the hearing of the plural number;
the consumption of ghee consists merely of bathing the body.
The particle "ca" (and) serves to draw in the act of *upasādana* (sitting near).
Therefore, having performed three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), consumed clarified butter (*ghṛta*), and performed the *upasādana*, one should study,
since no specific days of non-study (*anadhyāya*) are prescribed for this occasion.
And likewise when studying near a cremation ground, and likewise when studying near a cremation ground. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 1.66)
Āpastamba has stated that one should not study within the range of a *śamyā*-throw from all sides;
therefore, studying in its vicinity constitutes "studying at a cremation ground.
The prefix *abhi-* is intended to indicate that this is done intentionally.
Therefore, another expiation that is even lighter than the one [previously] mentioned should be understood as applying when [the offense] was unintentional.
And so Uśanas says: "In the case of reciting [the Veda] near a cremation ground without prior intent, one should recite after saying, 'Recite, sir!

By the word "and" (ca), there is the inclusion of everything previously mentioned, such as the *praṇāyāma* and so forth; however, by the word "thus" (evam), the inclusion is made specifically of the *upasadana* (approaching the teacher) mentioned immediately before.
If it is argued that, in that case, only the word *evaṃ* should be stated, we say no; for this meaning is obtained from both [words].
How so? When either the word *evaṃ* or the word *ca* ought to be stated, it is logical to assume a different purpose for the recitation of both.
For it is not [the case] that this applies to one person alone;
therefore, the *upasadana* (approaching the teacher) itself must be performed.

And so says another *smṛti*: "Having studied near a cremation ground, one should restrain the breaths, perform the touching of the breaths (*prāṇopasparśana*), the salutation (*abhivādana*), and the recitation of the *Sāvitrī*," and so forth.
The repetition is for the purpose of concluding the chapter.
All this expiation has been stated specifically for the pupil, because the study and other duties are for his sake.
Furthermore, in all cases, the penance consists precisely of approaching [the teacher];
"approaching" refers to salutation and so forth,
and that salutation is directed toward the teacher.
It is not possible.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
The second chapter. The initiation (*upanayana*) of the twice-born has been described.
Since some maintain that they possess the entitlement to certain duties of their social class even prior to initiation, he speaks as follows for that purpose:
Before the initiation ceremony, one may act, speak, and eat according to one's desire.
But surely this should have been stated even before initiation;
in that case, it would not be necessary to say "prior to initiation."
It is said: This is true;
however, the purpose for mentioning the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) at the beginning has already been stated.
It is not by this [statement] that it is enjoined.
Because it is already established by the sense;
nor is it restricted,
since there is no necessity for its performance.
This is because it will be stated later that "the rule begins with the initiation ceremony" (*upanayana*), and because there is no possibility of [the rule being] optional;
nor is it an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*).
Because there is an absence of cessation [of the offense],
for he has not incurred such things as being subject to the will of others;
therefore, this sutra is reiterative, intended to make known the absence of penance and royal punishment.
Because those two have been taught in a general manner.
But surely, royal punishments and penances are prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is prohibited;
yet this person has no entitlement (adhikāra) under either injunctions or prohibitions. Nor does he have an entitlement under injunctions or prohibitions.
And neither an injunction nor a prohibition for this [act] is heard; however,
it is not the case that its status as an *ahuta* (unoffered) act or the like will be enjoined or prohibited,
such that both [consequences] would arise upon its transgression.
Because [the knowledge] of the ancestors and others comes from instruction,
this sūtra is therefore purposeless.

To this it is replied: whatever expiation has been prescribed for the non-performance of what is enjoined or the practice of what is prohibited, or whatever royal punishment [is ordained], both of those apply to him as well.

Even though no specific injunction or prohibition is heard with reference to him alone, nevertheless, that which has been stated in general terms—such as "non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing," and so forth—[applies].
Since this [act] also possesses the nature of being a *tadvarṇa-dharma* (a duty pertaining to that specific class),
it follows that upon its transgression, both royal punishment and penance (*prāyaścitta*) apply.
Therefore, the Sūtra has been commenced in the form of a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of precluding that [consequence].
