By this sūtra, "The rule begins with the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*)," it will be stated that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) applies only to the transgression of that specific injunction which is prescribed starting from the initiation, and not to the transgression of others; therefore,
by that very [rule], one can understand that there is no expiation for the transgression of the duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*).
Even though there is an absence of royal punishment [in such cases], nevertheless,

for one who has passed the time for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), whose intellect is impaired, and who is capable [of performing duties], [the rule applies] from the eleventh year until before the sixteenth year for the purpose of entering into half the penance;
and prior to that, from after the fifth year, for the purpose of the father and others entering into the full penance.
Therefore, this sūtra has been commenced in order to demonstrate the absence of any fault prior to that age;
and thus it is said in the Bhārgavīya:
"He who is eighty years old, or a child less than sixteen..."
Women and those who are afflicted by disease deserve only half of the prescribed penance.
For one who is less than eleven years of age but more than five years old,
a friend or a teacher shall perform the penance for the sake of purification.
Therefore, for one who is even more ignorant than that, there is no offense anywhere;
consequently, neither royal punishment nor penance is prescribed for him.
Thus [it is said].

And thus, although it is generally appropriate for one to act according to his own will before the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), nevertheless, excessive freedom of action exists only prior to the age of five;
after that, he must be enjoined by his father and others to the duties of his social class (*varṇadharma*).
Because it is heard that when a child transgresses this, his father and others must undergo expiation;
enough of this digression.

Now the Sūtra is being explained: prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is freedom of action and movement according to one's will; therefore, regarding the touching of a Caṇḍāla and similar acts, he will state "merely sprinkling" (*avokṣaṇa*)—as in the phrase "from [the age of] sprinklings"—and it has been stated that even this applies only before the fifth year.
Beyond that [age], upon touching a Caṇḍāla or others, one must be bathed.
After the eleventh year, one should bathe by oneself;
this applies in all such cases.
"Speaking at will" means that one speaks even vulgarities and the like.
One belonging to the class of those who indulge in sensual pleasures may even eat food that has been kept overnight.
After the age of five, [the child] should be made to perform [ceremonies] that do not conflict with the duties of his caste.
The phrase "prior to the initiation ceremony" includes even the initiation ceremony performed in times of distress (*āpad-kalpa*).
Why? Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) "brahmacārī" (celibate student).

Since the observance of celibacy prior to the time of initiation is already established by the very impossibility of its transgression, the instruction regarding the protection of celibacy would be redundant.
He himself will provide an example of acting according to one's own desire: "He becomes one who voids urine and excrement wherever he happens to be."
Therefore, even during the stage of extreme childhood, one must strive to prevent [the child] from committing such acts as the killing of a Brahmin;

likewise, one must strive to prevent him from false accusations and the like, as well as from eating forbidden foods and drinking liquor (surā) and so forth, even during the stage of extreme childhood.

This is because, although the phrase "acting according to one's own will" (*kāmacāra*) already establishes this, the specific mention of "speech" (*vāda*) and "eating" (*bhakṣaṇa*) is repeated here for emphasis.
Although it should have been stated simply as "from the initiation ceremony" (*upanayanāt*), the inclusion of the word "prior to" (*prāk*) is for the purpose of restriction,
meaning that [the aforementioned behaviors] apply only prior to the initiation ceremony because of the freedom of action (*kāmacāritva*) [allowed] before it.
If this restriction were not present, [the rule] "and this is not in conflict with the subsequent ones" would follow.
By this [statement], the avoidance of eating the remnants of an oblation and other such practices would also apply to ascetics (yatis).
Now he states the exception regarding the consumption of food obtained through begging:
"A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) [may eat] from what has not been offered. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.2)
The *hutam* refers to what is offered and the remnants of the offering, such as the *caru* and *puroḍāśa*,
but not the remnants of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice, because that [remnant] serves all purposes.
Likewise, Āpastamba says: "One should make all [ancestors] sharers in the Vaiśvadeva.

The ellipsis is to be supplied as "from what is offered" (*ahutāt*). This is a prohibition of what would otherwise follow by implication; it is an instruction regarding the father and the other ancestors.
Because a child lacks discernment (*vijñāna*),
it is stated that [the responsibility] belongs to that very person once they are over eleven years of age.
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī). // Gautama 2.3 //
One must practice the preservation of celibacy.
Now he states an illustration of acting according to one's own will: "He passes urine and excrement wherever it may happen. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.4)
The meaning is that just as urine and feces are produced even when one has covered one's head while plowing and so forth, or while standing, one should do it in that very same way.
Furthermore, no rule for sipping water (ācamana) applies to him. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.5)
From five years of age until before the eleventh year, the ritual rule for *ācamana*—the procedure for sipping water—is not prescribed.
Because of the prohibition of the *kalpa* (ritual rule), it is understood that there is merely the act of *ācamana* itself.
In this regard, it is said: "Indeed, he is equal to a Śūdra as long as he is not born through the Veda."
Since it is heard in another Smṛti that one possesses duties equal to those of a Śūdra, the sipping of water (ācamana) should be understood to be like that of a Śūdra.
Why [is it said] "of one less than eleven years"?
Because the passage begins with the words "of this" (asya).
Because it is heard that there is an absence of fault prior to five years, and because one is entitled to the duties of one's caste (varṇadharma) after eleven years,
it is understood that even the rule for sipping water (ācamana) exists for him from the age of eleven onwards.
Now, regarding the very young child, he says:
"Except for wiping, running, and sprinkling. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.6)
The phrase "is not found for him" continues [from the previous rule].
The meaning is that for this child under five years of age, no other mode of purification exists apart from wiping and so forth.
"Wiping" (apamārjana) refers to the removal of food remnants from the mouth by means of the hand moistened with water.
Washing (*prakṣālana*) refers to cleansing after urination, defecation, and so forth;

sprinkling (*avokṣaṇa*) refers to the ritual sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) upon touching a *caṇḍāla* or similar person. Since [the fire] cannot be reached [by water], "no procedure for sipping water (*ācamana*) applies to it."
If it is argued that this results in the non-performance of the two prohibitions— "except for wiping, sprinkling, and pouring water"—
this is not a fault.

By the statement, "The rule for sipping water (ācamana) is not prescribed for him," the rule for sipping water is enjoined for one who is less than sixteen years of age by means of a prohibition regarding one who is less than eleven years of age;
[the exception being] "except for wiping, washing, and sprinkling."
Furthermore, by this [verse], the wiping and other rites for one who is less than five years old are prescribed by way of prohibiting other purificatory acts.
Furthermore:
"There is no impurity resulting from touching that [corpse]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.7)
By the mention of "that," one who has not yet performed purification is meant;
by touching such a person, or being touched by him, impurity does not arise. This rule applies specifically to very young children.
In that case, the prescription for its purification would be purposeless; why?
Because only two purposes for the prescription of purification are observed: to make it fit for contact with others, and for the sake of ritual performance.
However, this [purification] does not serve the purpose of making it fit for contact with others.
Because even one who has not performed purification is fit for contact,
as indicated by the statement, "There is no impurity from touching that";
and furthermore, it does not serve the purpose of ritual performance.
Because there is an absence of its performance.
It is not purposeless, because the prescription for purification is for the sake of protection;
likewise, another Smṛti states: "One should perform purification for the sake of protecting a child until the fifth year."
The use of the prefix *upa-* is intended to indicate the absence of fault when touching this very person while he has not yet performed purification;
thus, in the case of touching others who have become impure by food remnants, urine, or feces, one must perform ritual sipping (*ācamana*).
There is no fault in touching that [corpse], because it is enumerated among those touched by a corpse in the *Śavaspṛṣṭi-sūtra*. Likewise, another Smṛti states:
"He who touches one who is impure is indeed defiled alone."
Having touched it, another person would not be defiled; this is the rule regarding all objects.
Thus.
Regarding the touch of a Caṇḍāla, however, it will be stated in the Sūtra on touching a corpse:
"One should touch water";
yet, where it ought to have said "one should touch water," it says instead, "there is no impurity from touching him."
Thus, the rule regarding the making of a gurū-sūtra is intended to set aside even the restriction that it applies prior to initiation (*upanayana*);
consequently, even after initiation, one must perform *ācamana* upon touching what has been made impure by food remnants, or urine and feces.
Furthermore:
"But one should not employ him for the fire-oblation or the receiving of sacrificial offerings. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.8)
The word "this" (enam) is used for the purpose of including everyone who has not yet been initiated.

That which is performed in the fire, such as the Agnihotra oblation and so forth, is the *agnihavana*. That sacrificial offering (*bali*) which is given to the deities of the directions after the Vaiśvadeva rite is the *baliharaṇa*.
The word "tu" (but) expresses a distinction:

one should not employ [the mantra] even in the case of the Aṣṭakā and other rites, nor in such acts as washing the feet of a Brāhmaṇa; it applies specifically to the fire-oblation and the bali-offering.

The word "eva" (only) is used for this purpose: so that if one, being of a licentious nature, should study a mantra anywhere at all and proceed on his own accord to perform the Agnihotra and other rites, then even the one who permitted it would not be considered an approver.

This statement is intended to establish a rule for the initiated student (*upanīta*), because there is no possibility of such conduct occurring elsewhere, and thus it serves as a specific prohibition.
And thus, although by the scriptural injunction "one who knows [the ritual] should offer the Agnihotra," only one who has heard much (bahuśruta) is qualified, nevertheless,
in the absence of such a person, one should employ even one of little learning who has been initiated (upanīta).

And so Manu says: "Neither a maiden, nor a young woman, nor one of little learning, nor a fool, nor one who is afflicted, nor likewise one who is unconsecrated, shall be the *hotṛ* priest for the *agnihotra*."
Thus.

In that context, since the prohibition [of uninitiated status] is already established by the very prohibition of "having little learning" (*alpavidya*), the specific prohibition "not unrefined" (*nāsaṃskṛta*) is explained as being for the purpose of permitting even a refined person who possesses little learning, provided there is no other type of learned person.
As for what was stated previously regarding the period "before initiation" (*upanayana*) and so forth, that should be understood to apply to women as well until marriage.
Why? Because it is recorded in the tradition: "The rite of marriage is declared to be the initiation for women."
This is because of the observation of another Smṛti text.
In this way, the prohibition of *niyoga* for a maiden—even regarding the offering of oblations into the fire and the presentation of sacrificial food—is established.
Therefore, *niyoga* should be performed at a time subsequent to the marriage.

In this regard, because it is prohibited for a woman to perform the *agnihotra* by the Vedic injunction, "A woman shall not offer oblations," this [prohibition] should be understood to apply to the *aupāsana* sacrifice and similar rites.
Accordingly, another *smṛti* states: "The wife shall offer the *aupāsana* and the *vaiśvadeva*," and so forth.
And the prohibition "not a young woman" is not a fault, because it refers specifically to the wives of others.
Furthermore:
"One should not utter the word 'brahman' except when offering the *svadhā* libation. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.9)
The word "thus" (evam) is understood to carry over.
By the word "brahman," the Vedas are meant;
therefore, one should not teach him [the Veda].

Since the prohibition for one who has not been initiated is already established by the injunction for Vedic study— namely, "one who has been initiated should study the Vedas" after the *upākaraṇa* ceremony— the repeated prohibition of the Veda is for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), meaning that he must not be taught the Veda itself. Consequently, there is no fault in teaching him the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*).
One should not even utter a mantra that has been received through any manner whatsoever by acting according to one's own will;
why? Because the rule "one should cause [the student] to study" implies that it must be recited without having been commenced [independently].
This applies except for the offering of the *svadhā* libation.
Excluding the pouring of the *svadhā* offering:
having said "Svadhā to such-and-such," whatever is given to the deceased, such as the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) and water, that is the pouring of the *svadhā*.
This also serves as an indicative term for the entire ritual for the deceased.

And thus Vasiṣṭha says: "Except for water-rites, the svadhā-offering, and those connected with the ancestors. Consequently, even when a son exists though he is uninitiated (anupanīta), the funeral rites (pretakriyā) must not be performed by the sapinda relatives and others.
Lest there be the undesirable consequence that the injunctions of the scriptures would be rendered purposeless.
Having stated [the rules] for one who has not been initiated, he now speaks regarding one who has been initiated:
"The discipline begins with initiation" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.10).
The rule that has been stated beginning from the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is designated as "niyama" (observance).
Thus, in the case of its non-performance, there is an expiation (prāyaścitta), but not for the preceding [acts].

Or rather, starting from this point, the "niyama"—which will be described as the observance of vows (vratadhāraṇa) such as the kindling of the sacred fire (agnīndhana) and so forth—is the niyama; it must be performed beginning with the initiation ceremony.
Furthermore, the holy life (brahmacarya) has been explained. (Gautama 2.11)
The inclusion of the word "stated" (ukta) indicates that this [prohibition] is indeed a restrictive rule (*niyama*) prior to initiation (*upanayana*).

Consequently, in the event of a transgression of that rule, even for one who has not been initiated, it should be understood that his eligibility [for Vedic study] is restored solely through the penance prescribed for an *avakīrṇin* (one who has broken the vow of celibacy).
And so says another Smṛti: "One who has become corrupted should be purified by the vow of an *avakīrṇin* and initiated before he reaches the age of seventeen."
"Beyond this, [the penance is] by means of the vows for a Brātya and an Avakīrṇin.

If it is argued that for a religious student (brahmacārin), this is established by implication because of the prohibition against looking at women and so forth, we say no; for such acts are possible even with animals and the like.
Furthermore:
[The rules concerning] fire, fuel, and wandering for alms. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.12)
The kindling of the fire, the fuel, and the oblation—
these and the rest are well known.
These are to be performed every day.
The simultaneous instruction is for the purpose of performing [the acts] immediately thereafter;
and thus Manu says:
"Having received the desired staff and having worshipped the sun..."
Having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he should go about for alms according to the prescribed rule.
Thus [it is said].

In that context as well, it has been stated that by the phrase "having circumambulated the fire clockwise," the offering of fuel (samid-ādhāna) and the oblation (homa) are indicated. Furthermore: "In the evening and in the morning, one should eat food that has been honored and not disparaged."
Since it is heard that one should eat twice, it should be understood that the kindling of the sacred fires also occurs twice—in the evening and in the morning.
And so says another Smṛti:
"Having brought firewood from afar, he should place it in the open air."
One should offer oblations into the fire with those [verses] both in the evening and in the morning, remaining unwearied.
Thus;
some desire that the offering of fuel-sticks be performed only in the evening.
Moreover:
speaking the truth. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.13)
The phrase "the action to be performed" is to be supplied everywhere.
The explicit mention of the word "speech" (vacana) is for the sake of removing doubt; otherwise, there might be the doubt that "touching water" itself constitutes the truth.
The separate mention [of the sick person] is for the purpose of permitting their performance even when ill;
consequently, that [performance] does not apply to the two preceding cases.
And thus Manu says:
If one who is not ill fails to go on his alms-round or fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.
Thus [it is said].
Furthermore—touching water. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.14)
The mention of "ashes" (ab) is an elliptical expression intended to include ashes and other such substances.
Thus says Bhṛgu:
"Five meritorious baths have been proclaimed by the great seers."
The fire-born, the water-born, the Brahman-born, the wind-born, and likewise the celestial.

The fire-related bath is performed with ashes; the water-related bath is by immersion; the Vedic bath is performed with the mantra "āpo hi ṣṭhā"; and the wind-related bath is traditionally said to be [bathing] in the dust raised by cows.
That which consists of a divine year of heat is called the "divine bath" (divyasnāna).
If one is unable to perform the Varuṇa bath, one should perform the Āgneya or other [substitutes].
Thus.
Although one should have said simply "bathing" (*snāna*), the use of this specific term is for the purpose of including the rules for bathing mentioned in other Smṛtis.
And thus, that which is stated in other Smṛtis is to be understood here as well.
The prefix *upa-* is intended to exclude water that has not been properly examined.

The separate mention of "kindling the fire" and "wandering for alms" is for the purpose of prohibiting the daily bath after one has eaten, but not the occasional (naimittika) one. Therefore, the occasional bath must be performed.
The separate mention of "truthful speech" is for the purpose of prohibiting even a physician who acts as a messenger.
Some say that the prefix *upa-* is for the purpose of prohibiting bathing at midnight.
Whatever has been stated here has all likewise been stated by Manu:
One should not perform a bath after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight,
nor with one's clothes on, nor constantly, nor in an unknown body of water.
Thus it is said.
Some [say it consists of] the gift of a cow and so forth. (Gautama 2.15)
The Godāna, known as the second vow for the Chandogas, should also be observed by others in the sixteenth year;
some desire that even for them the Godāna be maintained in the sixteenth year. From that point onward, some desire the performance of the ceremonial bath (snāna).
Before the gift of a cow (godāna), one should not perform the daily bath (nityasnāna);
only the occasional bath (naimittika) should be performed. After that, some teachers maintain that the daily bath may also be performed.
Because of the expression "one," it is not Gautama.
And being outside the period of twilight. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.16)
The word "ca" (and) is for the purpose of carrying forward the mention of "some" (eke).
Some desire that the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) be performed outside the village,
but Gautama does not.
But Gautama does not hold this view.
What is meant is this: the opinion of some is that the twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) must be performed only outside the village;
whereas the opinion of Gautama is that it may be performed either outside or inside, in any pure place whatsoever.
Now, as a matter of context, [the author] states when and how that twilight worship (sandhyopāsana) should be performed:
"One should stand during the morning [twilight] and sit during the evening [twilight], remaining silent, as long as the light [of the sun or stars] is visible. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.17)
The term "vāgyataḥ" (restrained in speech) is connected with both "standing" and "sitting" individually.
That time at which the sun rises is the morning twilight (*pūrvā saṃdhyā*).
The word "saṃdhyā" is carried over from the preceding fragment of the sūtra.
That time at which the sun sets is the later twilight (*uttarā saṃdhyā*).
Here, standing and sitting are subordinate elements;
the act of worship (*upāsana*) is the primary rite here.
Therefore, although it is said "he should stand," it should nevertheless be understood that he should meditate while standing, and he should meditate while sitting.
And so Manu says:
"Standing while reciting the morning twilight prayer (saṃdhyā), one removes the sin committed at night;
but sitting for the evening one destroys the impurity created during the day."
Thus,
the time is "as long as the light remains," meaning until the light of the stars appears in the east.
The time that exists together with the light of the stars is "with light" (*sajyotis*); in that time which is "with light," the commencement [of the rite] should be performed.
For the other [time], it is likewise "with the light of the sun.
Therefore, "until the appearance of light" means until the appearance of the sun in the east and until the appearance of the stars in the west.
Although it should have been stated simply as "until light" (*ā jyotiṣaḥ*), the inclusion of the term "sight" (*darśana*) is for the purpose of completeness.
And so says Manu:
"The sages attained long life because of their prolonged observance of the *saṃdhyā*."
Wisdom, fame, renown, and indeed the splendor of sacred knowledge.
Thus it is said.

But is it not the case that by the rule "and this is not in conflict with the subsequent [rites]," this [practice] is not obtained for a *snātaka* who maintains the sacred fires (*agnimant*), because his time is already occupied by the fire-oblation (*agnihavana*)?
It is said: as for that smārta oblation performed in the evening and in the morning, there is indeed no contradiction because of the difference in time.
How so? By the word "evening" (sāyam), night is meant;
and by the word "morning" (prātaḥ), the day is meant.

Since there is no such statement here as in the case of the injunctions regarding the *uditahoma* (the oblation after sunrise), the *homa* would logically find its place immediately after the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*).

However, even though for some authorities the *homa* is prescribed at the very time of twilight, since "long twilight" (*dīrghasandhya*) is desired, there is still room for the twilight worship to occur even after the *homa*.
Thus, there is likewise no contradiction even regarding matters such as the offering of oblations prescribed in the Śruti.

Regarding the statement, "One should worship the morning twilight while standing and the evening twilight while seated," this phrasing is intended to include the injunctions stated in other Smṛtis as well.

Likewise, Uśanas says: "Having gone to water in the evening and the morning, having become pure and having cleansed oneself with a purifier, one should [worship] with the three verses beginning with 'āpo hi ṣṭhā,' with those verses that do not contain specific deity names (an-aliṅga), and with the Vāmadevya Sāman."
Then, seated on *darbha* grass in a pure place, holding *darbha* blades, facing west, and restraining his speech, he should meditate upon the Self.

Then, having performed three breath-controls (*prāṇāyāma*) consisting of exhalation (*recaka*), inhalation (*pūraka*), and retention (*kumbhaka*), he should repeat the *Sāvitrī* beginning with "Bhūḥ Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ" one thousand times, or one hundred times, or at least ten times, preceded by meditation on the *ṛṣi*, the meter (*chandas*), and the deity. Finally, rising, he should offer oblations to Agni, Yama, and Brahmā.
Having bowed to the west, south, and north, and having performed three circumambulations, one should again bow to the western direction.
In this very same manner, standing facing the east in the morning, one should bow to Mitra and the other deities.
Thus it is said.
One should not look at the sun.

If this prohibition were intended only for the two twilight periods (*sandhyā*), then a single sūtra would have been composed as follows: "One should stand during the former [twilight] and sit during the latter; one should remain until the stars appear, or until the light [of the sun] is seen; restrained in speech, one should not look at the sun.
If it were intended to apply at all times, then [the rule] "one should avoid honey and meat" would have been stated.
In such passages, one may also read "the gazing at the sun";
since it is not performed in either way, it can be understood that this was stated with another intention in mind.

And the underlying intention should be understood as stated in another Smṛti, just as Uśanas says: "One should not look at the sun when it has reached the twilight, when it is at midday, when it is eclipsed by Rāhu, or when it is reflected in water."

"One should avoid honey, meat, perfumes, garlands, sleeping during the day, collyrium, ointments, vehicles, shoes, umbrellas, lust, anger, greed, delusion, [excessive] speech, singing, bathing, cleaning the teeth, exhilaration, dancing, singing, slander, and fear"—
the verb "should avoid" is to be connected with each of these individually.
"Honey" refers to that produced by bees.
There is no fault in eating it unintentionally,
as seen in another Smṛti: "In the Vājasaneyaka, honey that comes about unintentionally does not cause impurity."
Although meat is not prohibited for a householder,
even in that case there is no fault in eating meat that is the leavings of one's teacher when it is for the sake of medicine for the sick, according to the rule:
"If he should fall ill, he may at will eat everything that is the leavings of his teacher for the purpose of medicine."
This is because of the observation of another Smṛti text.
Thus, it should be avoided even at a Śrāddha by one who is not ill.
And so says Manu:
In a rite dedicated to a deity, one may eat at will when invited for the sake of pleasure, as in the case of a *vratya* or a *ṛṣi*; his vow is not thereby violated.
And so forth. "Fragrance" refers to sandalwood and the like;
there is also a negation of that which has pleasure as its purpose.
It does not refer to what is left over by a deity, because another Smṛti text is seen which states: "A religious student should take only that which has been offered to a deity."
The same applies to wearing a garland as well.
Day-sleeping means indulging in sleep during the day; that too is not a fault for one who is ill.
"Collyrium for the eyes":
here too, there is a prohibition of its use for the sake of enjoyment, but not for the sake of medicine.
Anointing with oil means rubbing the limbs with oil.
Some say this is a prohibition specifically regarding scented oil; according to that view, there is no fault in using other types of oil.
If it is argued that this negation is established by the very negation of "fragrance" (gandha), we say no;
for due to specific worldly convention, there is no apprehension of the general category (sāmānya) of fragrance [by the term "smell"].
"Vehicle" (yāna) refers to a palanquin and the like.
That too applies only to one who is not ill;
sandals and umbrellas are well-known [exceptions],
and there is no fault in using one made of peacock feathers.
Lust is the desire for enjoyment directed toward women; anger is the contemplation of harm toward another;
greed is the unjust seizure of another's property and so forth.
Delusion is ignorance; idle chatter is excessive prattle;
playing instruments refers to the beating of drums and so forth.
Bathing refers to bathing the head and so forth, by which one enjoys [the ritual];
this is because the other [types of bathing] are prescribed [for specific occasions].
Cleansing the teeth is well known.
This must not be done even with a betel leaf, because another Smṛti text states: "The observer of the vow shall have teeth free from [stained] mud.
Joy (*harṣa*) means delight; thus, it is established that there is also a prohibition against watching the causes of such joy, such as plays (*nāṭaka*) and the like.
Because joy arises upon seeing that [object], it is impossible to prevent it;
*nṛtta* is the movement of the limbs,
and *gīta* is the utterance of words related to music (*gāndharva*).
Slander is the proclamation of another's faults.
Fear is the intimidation of another, because it cannot be avoided by anyone else.
Furthermore:

when in the presence of a teacher, one must not cover the neck, nor sit with the knees bound by a cloth (avasakthika), nor lean against a support, nor stretch out the feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.20)
"Guru" refers to the preceptor (ācārya) and others.
Why? If only the preceptor were intended, then one should have said "seeing the preceptor" (ācāryadarśana).
The inclusion of the term "guru" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) that includes all those who occupy the position of a guru.
And so another Smṛti states: "He should remain with his limbs contracted in the presence of all those who are arrogant. Covering the neck (*kaṇṭhaprāvaraṇam*) means throwing a cloth around the neck.
*Avasakthikām* refers to tying a girdle-like band above the knees.
The rest is well known.
Since these [actions] are performed under the control of another, they are prohibited.
Furthermore:
spitting, laughing, yawning, and cracking the knuckles. (Gautama Sūtra 2.21)
It is mentioned separately for the purpose of avoiding it both in the presence of the guru and in the presence of others.
Spitting is well known [as improper]. Even when under the influence of another, laughter must be avoided with effort.
And likewise Āpastamba says: "One should not smile; if one should smile, one should smile after covering [the mouth]," according to the Brāhmaṇa.
Yawning is well known.
Snapping the fingers is the forceful release of a joint accompanied by sound.
Furthermore:
"And upon seeing or obtaining a woman, when there is suspicion of sexual intercourse. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.22)
The word "should avoid" (varjayet) carries over from the previous context.
"Gazing" (prekṣaṇa) means looking intently, that is, the detailed examination of the individual parts,
not merely the sight of the form itself.
Because it is impossible to prevent its blinking,
"ālambana" means touching (*sparśana*). Although one could have said "in touching," this specific expression is used for the purpose of excluding intentional touching.
Thus, there is no fault due to negligence;
however, even in the dark and so forth, one should not touch [it] intentionally.
One should not perform either of these two acts with regard to a woman.
In that very [woman] regarding whom others have a suspicion of sexual intercourse, and not in another.
Gambling, service to the low, taking what is not given, and violence. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.23)
"One should avoid" is the essential point.
Gambling refers to playing with dice and the like. Service to the lowly refers to service such as cleaning away urine and excrement.
And likewise, even toward a teacher, service that is inappropriate should not be performed.
Taking what is not given (*adattādāna*) means taking even that which has been discarded without being permitted.
Violence (*hiṃsā*) means the killing of living beings or the infliction of suffering upon them.
One should neither cause [a ritual] to be performed out of season, nor even give one's consent for it.
Furthermore:
the names of the teacher, his son, his wife, and one initiated [into a Vedic school] (Gautama 2.24).
The subject at hand is that one should avoid [pronouncing names].
One should not utter the names—such as those given by a father or others—of the teacher, his son, his wife, or one who has been initiated.
Furthermore:
"Acid words [are to be avoided]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.25)
One should avoid all those who are harsh, cruel, and who cause agitation to others.
A Brāhmaṇa must always abstain from intoxicants. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.26)
"One should avoid" is the subject under discussion.
A Brāhmaṇa should always avoid liquor—whether made from molasses, honey, or flour, or any other intoxicant—even prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Likewise, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, there is no prohibition against *surā* (liquor) other than that made from flour (*paiṣṭī*), both before and after initiation until the period of studentship (*brahmacarya*) has ended.
This is because it is seen in another Smṛti;
as Manu said:
"Surā should be known to be of three kinds: that made from molasses (gauḍī), that made from honey (mādhvī), and that made from flour (paiṣṭī)."
Just as one [is not to be drunk], so all [are not to be drunk] by the best of the twice-born.
Thus it is said.
Now, in order to set forth what ought to be done, he says:
"He should sleep on a low bed, rise before [others], and be the last to go to rest. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.27)
In relation to the guru, one should use a lower bed and seat;
one should rise before him and go to rest after him.
As Manu has said:
In the presence of his teacher, his bed and seat should always be low;
he should rise before him and go to rest after him.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore:
"He is restrained in speech, arms, and stomach. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.28)
The word "syāt" (should be) is understood as the ellipsis.
One who is restrained in speech is one who has desisted from idle chatter.
One who is restrained in the arms is one who avoids crushing clods of earth and similar acts.
"Restrained in the stomach" means eating what is wholesome and moderate;
some read the text as "restrained in the actions of speech, arms, and stomach."
Since that [result] is already established by the mere fact of being bound by his arms, it must be investigated whether this is appropriate or inappropriate.
Furthermore, one should mention the name and lineage of the teacher with respect. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.29)
The mention of "guru" is an elliptical expression that includes the preceptor (*ācārya*) and others as well.
"From the same" means from one who is properly bowed;
it means having meditated upon him and performed a salutation.

And thus, even there, in the expression "the teacher and his son," the mention of "teacher" is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa) of the preceptor and others as well, because the utterance of their names is likewise prohibited.
And so another Smṛti states: "The teacher, his son, his wife, one initiated as a guru, the father, the paternal uncle, the mother, and likewise the maternal uncle."
A wise man should not mention by name his father-in-law, his husband, or his mother’s sister, even if they are well-wishers and learned.
But if he should speak, one should meditate upon him, pay homage, and then address him.
Thus [it is said].
And likewise for one who has been honored and for one who is superior. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.30)
The meaning is that he is one who is honored, worthy of respect, and learned. He should be understood as being superior, a well-wisher, and advanced in age;
for although this is already established by the word "and" (ca), the word "thus" (evaṃ) serves the purpose of extending [the rules] to this entire case.
And therefore, whatever [rites] such as salutation are prescribed upon seeing the Guru, those should be understood to apply here as well.
Having left behind his bed, seat, and dwelling place, he should give his assent.
When the Guru gives the command, then "bed" refers to a couch and the like;
"seat" refers to a wooden plank and the like;
and "place" refers to where one is situated.
The meaning is that, having set aside and abandoned these, one should give a response, that is, a reply.
One should approach [the teacher] upon being called, even if one is not seen by him. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.32)
The meaning is that when an instruction is being given by an invisible teacher, one should perform an "approach," which is to go toward him.
One should rise upon seeing one's teacher, as well as when passing by those situated below, on a seat, or moving horizontally, or when encountering a crosswind. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.33)
When the teacher stands or sits below or at a lower level,
or when one is exposed to crosswinds or engaged in the voiding of urine or feces,
upon seeing the teacher there, one should rise.
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it means having turned one's face away from the other.
And so it is said in another Smṛti:
"Upon seeing the Guru standing at a well, or likewise standing at a pond..."
The disciple, as well as the servant, should remain standing with their faces turned away from him.
Thus it is said.
Alternatively, by the word "and" (ca), departure is also expressed.

In that case, the meaning of the Sūtra should be understood as follows: "In the event of [the presence of] one sitting below, one sitting on a seat, or the use of crosswinds, one should rise and depart in due order. Here, the sequence is: upon seeing someone sitting below or on a seat, one should rise; and in the case of the use of crosswinds, one should depart.
One should follow one who is walking. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.34)
"Seeing him going, one should follow.
The word "and" (ca) carries over;
by it, even that which is not explicitly stated is included: seeing him seated, one should rise; seeing him lying down, one should sit.
And so another Smṛti states: "One should follow him as he walks, stand when he sits, and sit near him when he lies down."
Having made known one's action, [one should confess it]. (Gautama 2.35)
Having informed the teacher, "I shall perform whatever task is to be done by him," and having performed it, he should remain standing after announcing, "It is done.
Because the sentence is incomplete, the word "having performed" (*kṛtvā*) must be supplied after "having informed" (*vijñāpya*);
likewise, the verb "should remain" (*tiṣṭhet*) is to be supplied after "having announced" (*ākhyāya*).
It is like the expression: "Enter the rice-ball."
One who studies when summoned [to do so]. // Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.36 //
The meaning is that he should study only when summoned by the teacher; he should not, however, urge him [to study].
He should be intent upon what is pleasant and beneficial. // Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.37 //
The word "syāt" (might be) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Devoted to that" means intent upon both the pleasant and the beneficial in combination.
Because that which is beneficial but unpleasant should not be done: "pleasant" means causing delight,
and "beneficial" means enduring for the future.
The meaning is that one should do only that which is both pleasing and conducive to the future.
And the same applies to his wife's sons. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.38)
He should also be intent upon the welfare and benefit of those two who are his wife and son, provided they are of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and similar to him;
by the use of the word "also" (*ca*), items such as a neck-cloth are included.
If it is asked why only those of the same caste are mentioned, it is because the plural number is used for the sake of honor.
Now he states an exception to that rule:
"There shall be no eating of leftovers, bathing [him], adorning him, washing his feet, massaging him, or clasping his feet. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.39)
One should not perform these for his wife or son; although they would otherwise be required because of their being dear and beneficial, they are here prohibited.
Since these are specifically forbidden for these two, it follows that for one's teacher, these must indeed be performed.
Likewise, Āpastamba states: "One who has gone abroad should eat after having offered alms-food into the fire; alms-food is praised as being equivalent to sacrificial oblation (havis).

In that regard, the teacher serves as the deity and for the purpose of the Āhavanīya fire; having fed him, whatever remains as leavings he eats—that is indeed the leavings of the sacrificial oblation," and so forth.
Similarly, Vasiṣṭha also says: "The leavings of one who is not one's guru are not to be eaten," and so forth.
Adornment (*prasādhana*) means ornament (*alaṃkāra*).
The rest is well known.
Now he states an exception to the rule regarding salutation:
"Upon returning from a journey, one should salute the wives of one's gurus. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.40)
One who has returned from a journey abroad must perform the salutation by clasping the feet of his teacher’s wives;
not at any other time,
nor toward the wives of anyone else.
But even there, one should not [behave] with young women who have reached the age of marriage. (Gautama 2.41)
The meaning is: "by one who is capable of legal transactions" and "who has reached the full age of sixteen years.
Some maintain that for young women—that is, for maidens—even after returning from travel, [the rite] should not be performed; however, Gautama does not hold this view.
It should be understood in consideration of both those things that are to be suspected and those that are not to be suspected.
It was stated: "Regarding fire, fuel, and the practice of begging.
In that context, since fire and fuel are obtained separately from householders alone, he now states the rule for the practice of begging:
He may wander for alms among all castes, with the exception of those who are accused of crimes and those who have fallen from their status.

For what purpose is this Sūtra commenced? To begin with, the practice of wandering for alms is not enjoined by this [Sūtra], because it has already been enjoined by the rule: "The kindling of the sacred fires and the practice of wandering for alms."
And the avoidance of those whose husbands have been accused [of infidelity] is because it has already been stated by the phrase "those who are not praised in their own duties."

On this point, some say: "This undertaking is for the purpose of including the Śūdra, because [the status of the Śūdra] was not established by the rule, 'Those who are praiseworthy in their own duties'."
And this is not tenable,
because the permission for a Śūdra woman is already established by the rule, "If there is no [other] wife, then [one may take] one from among Śūdras," which applies to times of distress (*āpad*).
Nor is it appropriate to infer from this that a student (*brahmacārin*) is permitted to have a Śūdra wife even when not in a state of distress.
In another Smṛti, because it is absolutely prohibited:
"One whose limbs are nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, even if he constantly studies, performs fire-sacrifices, or recites prayers, does not attain the higher state."
Thus it is said.

Therefore, this undertaking is intended solely for the purpose of permitting a student (*brahmacārin*) to approach a censurable member of the twice-born classes when no other occasion arises; for since the approach to all censurable persons would otherwise apply without distinction, the prohibition "excepting those accused of grave sins and the outcasts" is appropriate.

Otherwise, if the approach were restricted to Śūdras alone, there would be no possibility of approaching those such as the "accused," and thus the prohibition would be illogical. Furthermore, it cannot be argued that this exception applies exclusively to the case of a Śūdra.
For where the twice-born are prescribed as qualified, there the Śūdra is also indeed prescribed; thus, there is no possibility at all for the other [case].
Accordingly, in the first case, the student should practice begging for alms from those who are commendable;
if those are unavailable, from those who are not commendable;
and if even those are unavailable, from the teacher and others.
It is established that in the absence of all [other options] during a time of distress, one may [accept food] from a Śūdra.
"Sārvavarṇika" means fit for all castes (*sarvavarṇa*); the meaning is that it belongs to everyone.
The inclusion of the term "all" is for the purpose of including the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas.

Otherwise, since only a Brāhmaṇa would have the entitlement to receive gifts, it would belong to him alone. The mention of "caste" (varṇa) is for the purpose of extending [the entitlement] to the Śūdra as well; for if the term "caste" were not used, the inclusion of "all" (sarva) would apply only to those two [the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya]. Therefore, the mention of "caste" is made so that it may apply to the Śūdra, who would otherwise not be included. Thus, the mention of "caste" is intended to extend [the rule] to the Śūdra.
Consequently, there is no fault in a Śūdra who is destitute of a livelihood resorting to begging;
*bhaikṣa* is a collection of alms,
and therefore it should be gathered from many houses.

"One accused" (abhiśasta) refers to one accused of the fault of a minor offense (upapātaka), since one accused of the fault of a major sin (pātaka) is already covered by the mention of the "outcast" (patita).
Thus says Vasiṣṭha: "Having falsely accused a Brāhmaṇa of a sin causing loss of caste (patanīya) or a sin not causing loss of caste (upapatanīya)."
Some analyze the term as *sārvavarṇika*, meaning "belonging to all castes" (*sarveṣu varṇeṣu bhavam*). For them, we do not see the purpose of including the word "all" (*sarva*).
If it is intended to include those of inferior twice-born status, that cannot be so, because that very purpose would already be served by the commencement of the Sūtra itself.
Even if the purpose were to include Śūdras, the same refutation has already been stated. Therefore, this matter should be investigated by those learned Brahmins (*bhūsura*s).
The word *bhava* (existence) should be employed at the beginning, middle, and end [of the recitation], according to the sequence of the syllables.

In the request "Give alms to a two-footed one," since the word *dehi* (give) is also obtained through the force of the imperative suffix, the word *bhavat* (sir) should be employed at the beginning by a Brāhmaṇa,
in the middle by a Kṣatriya, and at the end by a Vaiśya.

Since the word *bhavat* is a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) and cannot be used in isolation, it must be employed in the vocative case when addressing women, as in: "O lady (*bhavati*), give alms. When addressing men, it is used as: "O sir (*bhavan*), give alms."
Following the prefix *pra*, one should also observe what is stated in another Smṛti:
"In that case as well, the letters *kṣa* and *hri* should not be pronounced loudly.
As the Gṛhya-smṛti says: "A Brāhmaṇa should beg, saying, 'Sir, give alms.'"
"A Kṣatriya [begs] with the middle word 'bhavat'—[saying], 'O lady, give alms'; a Vaiśya [begs] with the final word 'bhavat'—[saying], 'Lady, give alms, please';
and he should not add 'kṣām' and 'hiṃ'."

The mention of "caste" (varṇa) is for the purpose of including the Śūdra in the attainment of mantras; consequently, it should be understood that one of the mantras belonging to the three castes alone is to be used,
or else another specific composition must be made.
Because another Smṛti states, "The Śūdra’s livelihood is like that of the Vaiśya," it should be understood as being the same as what was prescribed for the Vaiśya.
A specific mantra was not explicitly mentioned for the purpose of indicating that his livelihood is unrestricted.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "And his livelihood is unrestricted; his hair and dress are unrestricted," and so forth.
The mention of "successive" is for the purpose that there should not be a conceptual construction of [the object] as a single unit.
In the absence of [these], one may do so with others, except for the teacher, a kinsman, a preceptor, or one's own [parents].
The teacher said:
"A kinsman is one who shares the sapinda relationship; a guru is one such as a maternal uncle and so forth."
"Own" means belonging to oneself.
If it cannot be obtained elsewhere, alms should be requested from these [persons].
The sequence, however, has already been established.
In this case as well,
one should avoid each preceding one of those [faults] first.
Whichever among them is first mentioned in each case, one should avoid that;
however, if nothing else is obtained, even after avoiding the preceding ones, one should continue to seek alms from those very same individuals.
The mention of these [other sources] is for the purpose of establishing a restriction, namely that [one should not seek alms] from the teacher's house alone.
Consequently, it should be understood that in the event of failure to obtain [alms] anywhere else, one may indeed do so from the teacher's house.
Thus, another Smṛti states: "In the event of failure to obtain [alms] elsewhere, even from the teacher's house."
Having offered [the food] to his teacher and being permitted by him, he should eat. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.46)
Having announced to the teacher, "This is the alms-food," he should eat it only when permitted by him with the words, "Eat.
Thus, this announcement is for the purpose of consecrating the alms-food,
as indicated by the expression "permitted."
If the teacher should take it, then another must be brought.
In his absence, [the debt shall be paid] by his wife, son, fellow student, or a virtuous person.
In the presence of the teacher, an announcement should be made regarding his wife and others as appropriate.
The mention of "his" (tad-) is for the purpose of indicating that the wife and son must belong to the same caste.
A *sabrahmacārī* is one who follows the same branch of study (*caraṇa*).
A "good" person is one who possesses excellent qualities.
Regarding how one should eat that, he says:
"Restraining his speech, being satisfied, and not being greedy, having placed water nearby. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.48)
"Restrained in speech" means silently; "being satisfied" means practicing contentment—
the sense being that even if one was previously dissatisfied, one should rejoice at the mere sight of food.
And so another Smṛti says:
"Upon seeing [the guest], one should rejoice, be gracious, and welcome him in every way."
Thus,
the meaning is that one who is not being led astray, avoiding the longing for specific [delicious] foods, should abstain from overeating.
And so it is said in another Smṛti:
Excessive eating is detrimental to longevity, detrimental to health, and detrimental to strength.
It is demeritorious and loathed by the world; therefore, one should avoid it.
Thus [it is said].
Alternatively, the meaning is "without avoiding the rules for eating.
Accordingly, the rules for eating should be observed in another Smṛti.
The meaning is that one should sip water while reciting "samyaṅ.
The prefix *sam-* is intended to include the procedure mentioned in other Smṛtis.
Thus, Uśanas says: "One should sprinkle water with [the mantra] beginning 'satyaṃ tvartena,' and then cause [the person] to sip it with [the mantra] beginning 'amṛtopastaraṇam.'"
Alternatively, "water" refers to a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*); having placed that [nearby],
it follows that even a religious student (*brahmacārin*) must carry a water-pot.
In the same way, Manu also indicates the carrying of a water-pot by the religious student (*brahmacārin*), since he prescribes its disposal along with the girdle and other items:
"Having thrown into the water the girdle, the antelope skin, the staff, the sacred thread, and the water-pot when they are worn out, one should take others according to the prescribed mantras."
Thus, in this manner, the sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed from that very [source],
by virtue of the force of the scriptural statement.
There is no fault in touching what has been left over from a meal;
or rather, one should look to what is stated in another Smṛti.
As Vasiṣṭha says:
Fire is considered pure when prepared from water, from the hand, or from wood;
therefore, one should wipe the water-pot with both hands and water.
Thus,
some support this meaning by means of the prefix itself.
Now, if a religious student (brahmacārī) should abide in proper discipline toward his teacher, what then should be done? To this he says:
"The instruction of the pupil is by means of non-corporal punishment. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.49)
The instruction of disciples means the disciplining of disciples;
the meaning is that it should be carried out through methods such as reprimand, excluding physical punishment.

Since this is already established by the context of the qualification (*adhikāra*), the mention of "disciple" (*śiṣya*) is for the purpose of making it known that this very same duty applies to others who are to be instructed, such as a wife, a son, and so forth.
If one is unable [to do so], one may use thin strips of rope or split bamboo.
If instruction through reprimand and other such means is ineffective, one may use a rope or a split bamboo cane;
since these two are mentioned together, they are optional alternatives because they serve the same purpose.
Even with that, the student should be instructed gently.
If he strikes with something other [than the prescribed means], he should be punished by the king.
One who strikes with anything other than the hands or feet out of anger shall be punished by the king;
the mention of the "king" is for the sake of showing respect.
Now, as to how long he should observe this [vow], he says:
"He should practice the life of a religious student (brahmacarya) for twelve years regarding one Veda. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.52)
One who is about to study a single Veda shall practice— that is, observe— for twelve years the student's life (*brahmacarya*) as previously described.
By the term *brahmacarya*, the entire collection of restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) is meant, because it is for the sake of Brahman.
Or up to twelve [times]. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.53)
Or he should practice the life of a student for twelve years for each Veda.
Or, in all cases, [the period lasts] until the completion of the formal initiation (grahaṇa).

For as long as it takes to complete the study of all the Vedas, for that same length of time one should observe the life of a religious student (brahmacarya), because that is the purpose of such study. The inclusion of the word "all" is for the sake of indicating whether one studies one, two, or indeed all of them.
And so says Manu:
Having studied the Vedas—whether all four, two, or even one—in due order.
Thus,

this is an exception (apavāda) regarding the previously stated limit, whether it be subsequent or prior; and the statement concerning the rule (niyamokti) is that what is studied according to this rule becomes efficacious (vīryavat).
At the conclusion of his studies, the teacher should be invited by the student with a gift.
Upon the completion of his studies, but not necessarily upon the completion of his vows,
the student should invite the preceptor— the teacher— with a purpose or motive, asking: "What may I do for the sake of my guru?"
Then, having performed the bath, he may either remain as permitted or bathe again. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.56)

"Having performed" means having given; that is, the object instructed by the teacher. Or, for one who has been permitted with the words "Enough with this gift to the teacher," the ritual bath is the *samāvartana*.
Now, regarding the question of which among many gurus—such as one's father and others—is to be honored first when they are present together, he says:
"The teacher is the most excellent of all gurus. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.57)
The teacher (ācārya) is defined by the characteristics already mentioned; he is the most excellent and preeminent among all gurus, including others such as one's father and so forth.
Consequently, [the rule applies] "in the case of a collision with another."
In this context, it is precisely this [subject] that is denoted by the word "other" (para).
"Some say 'Mother,' some say 'Mother. (Gautama 2.58)
Some consider the mother to be superior;

others [consider] the father [superior], because of the use of the particle *iti*. Otherwise, since [the meaning] "the mother alone" would already be established [by the word *mātā* itself], [the particle *iti* would be redundant].
The teacher is more important than the father alone;
thus says Manu:
"That which the mother and father produce for him through their union out of desire..."
One should know that to be his true origin from which he is born in a womb.
But whatever birth the teacher, who has mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule by means of the Sāvitrī, that is real; it is ageless and immortal.
Thus,
if the father alone is the teacher, then the father is distinguished;
however, the mother is the most excellent of all.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "An Ācārya is ten times more venerable than an Upādhyāya, a father is a hundred times more venerable than an Ācārya, and a mother exceeds a father a thousandfold in respect."
In this context, by the word "father" (pitṛ), only that teacher who is actually one's father is intended.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
The Third Chapter: Regarding one who has thus fulfilled his vows and completed his studies, some authorities state that there is an option concerning his stage of life (*āśrama*).
Of him whose brahmacarya has remained unbroken;
and so Manu says:
"Having studied the Vedas, or two Vedas, or even one Veda, in due order..."
Having remained inviolate in his vow of celibacy, he should enter the stage of life of a householder.
Thus,
the penance for a minor offense (*upapātaka*) should be understood as applicable to one who has been thus corrupted;
or else, that specific mention is intended to exclude the Śūdra.
Or rather,
the phrase "of each" (tasya tasya) is used for the sake of distributive repetition,
meaning "of the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya," so that it may not be thought that this [definition] applies only to the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma).
If it is argued that this is established by the very context even without mentioning him [the Brāhmaṇa], we say no;
for its purpose is to remove the suspicion that this might be a spurious Smṛti.
For another Smṛti appears thus: “This fourfold dharma of the Brāhmaṇa has been declared to you.”
In this regard, one might suspect that this fourfold dharma belongs exclusively to the Brahmin, while for the other two [castes] it is of only one kind.
If it is asked, "How then is that so?", the mention of the "Brahmin" there is for the sake of illustration.
If it is further asked, "How is this understood? it is because another Smṛti text shows that the four stages of life (āśramas) belong to all three castes.

And likewise Āpastamba says: “For all [orders], residence in the teacher’s family is the same from the initiation onwards; for all, there is no departure until the knowledge [of the Veda] has been attained; having understood the duties, one may undertake whatever one desires.
Some say that because their fruits are equal, there is an option regarding the stages of life (āśrama).
For there are two kinds of fruit: that which consists of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and that which consists of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
These are obtained by means of either one of these [paths].

Thus says the Śruti: “There are three branches of dharma: sacrifice, study, and charity—this is the first; austerity alone is the second; and dwelling in the teacher’s family is the third. Having ascended these, one goes to the world of Brahman.”
"One established in Brahman attains immortality.
As for the meaning: there are three supports of Dharma—the sacrifice, study, and giving; this is the instruction regarding the householder.
"Austerity alone" refers to the duty of the forest-dweller and the wandering mendicant; "dwelling in the teacher's family" refers to the student;
and "having ascended these" refers to the stage of the student.

The meaning is: having properly entered either the stage of the householder (gṛhasthāśrama), the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprasthāśrama), or the stage of the wandering mendicant (parivrājakāśrama).
Among them, he who is established in Brahman, devoted to Brahman,
and possessed of knowledge, attains— that is, goes to— immortality, which is liberation.
Furthermore, because it is taught that all [of these stages] lead to the attainment of the world of Brahman (*brahmaloka*), it is stated that they possess an identical fruit.
Likewise, in the Jābāla Śruti as well, an identical fruit is heard: "Having completed the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*), one should become a householder."
"Having been a householder, one should become a forest-dweller; having been a forest-dweller, one should go forth.
Or otherwise, one may go forth directly from the life of a student, or from the home, or from the forest; thus one goes to the world of Brahman."
Manu also said:
"All these [stages of life], when practiced in succession according to the scriptures,
lead a Brahmin who acts as prescribed to the supreme goal."
Thus [it is said].
Here too, because of the word "api" (also/even), one [additional stage] is also to be understood.
Āpastamba also says: "There are four stages of life: the householder's state, dwelling in the teacher's family, the state of the silent sage (mauna), and forest-dwelling (vānaprasthya)."
"By proceeding without distraction among all of these according to the instruction, one attains security";
thus, because they yield an equal result, there is an option (vikalpa).

[Objection: But if they are equal, since both kinds of fruits would be attained through *brahmacarya* alone, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the injunctions for the other stages of life (*āśrama*) are purposeless. [Reply:
It is said in response: the injunction of the other stages of life is for the sake of those who are capable of practicing them, so as to enter those respective stages;
or else, it is for the sake of entering the desired stage of life through the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous births.
The scripture states: "Knowledge and action, as well as prior wisdom, accompany him.
Furthermore, the scriptural injunction regarding lifelong [performance of rites] is to be understood as applying to the householder who possesses desire and is capable.

When this is so accepted, the scriptural passage concerning renunciation also becomes consistent: "Having thus known that Self, one rises above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then leads the life of a mendicant."
[They] "move about";

for otherwise, the instruction for renunciation (saṃnyāsa) as "the practice of begging" would not be tenable. Furthermore, by the scriptural passage concerning birth, the necessity of performing sacrifices and other rites for the householder is established.
But it does not apply to one who is merely being born,

because the connection with the three debts is absolutely impossible [in that case], and because it would contradict the Vedic revelation stating, "One should renounce even from the stage of studentship"; thus, "He renounces from that very stage of studentship."

Furthermore, this is not contradicted by such Smṛti texts as, "In whichever [place] one desires, there one should dwell," and because explanatory passages (arthavādas) are supplementary to what is to be performed.
Furthermore, the meaning of the passage should be understood as follows: a householder, being born, enters the state of householdership through his prior latent impressions (*pūrvavāsanā*).
The mention of the *brahman* (Brahmin) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya.
He becomes bound by three debts: he becomes indebted to the gods through sacrifice; therefore, sacrifice must be performed.
"From this [debt] to the ancestors by means of progeny," therefore, the procreation of offspring must be performed;
"from this [debt] to the seers by means of celibacy," therefore, the observance of celibacy must be maintained on the days of the lunar nodes and other such occasions.
When understood in this way, there is no contradiction anywhere between the Śruti and the Smṛti.
Because of the mention of "some" (eke), however, Gautama is not included;
rather, his [view] is considered to be a cumulative combination.
How is this understood?

Because the view that there is only one stage of life (*aikāśramya*) is presented as the opinion of others (*paramata*) even in the section refuting [the four stages] with the words "But the teachers [hold] to one stage of life," and because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating "There are three stages of life prior to the last one," the triad [of stages] does not exist prior to the final stage of life.
Regarding the position of the alternative view, Gautama considers it thus:
"Through sacrifice one attains the gods; through austerity, the Vairāja state;
through renunciation, the abode of Brahman; and through dispassion, dissolution into Prakṛti."

Thus, because they are taught as having distinct results; because even in the Jābāla Śruti, instead of saying "having ascended any one of them," it says "having ascended these [all]," thereby indicating the intention of their combination;

because the attainment of the world of Brahman is also taught as the result of their combination; and because even in the Jābāla Śruti, the position of combination itself was stated first as being primary—[it follows that] "all [the paths] lead in succession."
In this statement of Manu, because the word "api" (also/even) has the sense of conjunction;

and in the statement of Āpastamba, because of the plural "teṣu sarveṣu" (in all of those), which is spoken with the intention that [the debt] does not reside in only one, but rather resides in all of them; and because the scriptural mention of the three debts is also established as being exactly according to the literal meaning—[therefore, the father must perform the sacrifice].
Because the scriptural statement, “and his former knowledge,” is also consistent with the intention of referring to *vidyā* (spiritual knowledge);

because even the *yāvajjīva* (lifelong) injunction is seen to be non-permanent in the Jābāla Śruti passage, “If a householder enters the forest, and if he should desire the household life itself, then he should perform the *agnihotra* for as long as he lives”;
and because, on this view, the scriptural statement regarding the suspension [of rites] is all the more easily established.

Since even by this [verse], "the fourth part of his life," Manu has spoken while relying precisely on the position of cumulative performance (*samuccaya*), the position of cumulative performance alone is superior.
For this very reason, the positions of option (*vikalpa*) and sublation (*bādha*) have been presented as the views of others.

And thus, statements such as "he may dwell in whichever [place] he desires" should be understood as having been spoken from the perspective of an option for one who is incapable of performing [the rites] in combination (samuccaya) due to defects such as blindness or lameness, or due to poverty and the like. This is stated with the intention that such a person must resort to the alternative of option (vikalpa), even though this is already established by implication.
Alternatively, the one who possesses knowledge of the inner self (adhyātmajñānin) should resort to the alternative of option.
The other [view] is the position of their combination. Why? Because the purpose of the performance [of rituals] is the arising of knowledge;
once that has arisen, the human goal is accomplished for a person regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) they abide in.
The mention of "stages of life" (āśrama) is for the sake of conventional usage, as in such passages as "the castes and the stages of life."
What, then, are those stages of life? To this he says: "The student, the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.2)
One who practices celibacy (*brahmacarya*),
or one who moves about without longing for the very domain of Brahman, is a *brahmacārī*.
A house is [defined by] a wife; one who possesses that through union with her is a householder (*gṛhastha*).
One who subsists on alms and so forth is a mendicant (*bhikṣu*). The scripture proclaimed by Vikhanas is the *Vaikhānasa*; one who conducts himself according to its rules is a *vaikhānasa*.

This irregularity is for the purpose of indicating their distinctness, just as Uśanas says: "There are two types of religious students (brahmacārin): the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) and the temporary student (upakurvāṇa)."

"There are two types of Vaikhānasas: those with wives and those without wives; two types of renunciants (saṃnyāsins): the mendicant-renunciant (bhikṣusaṃnyāsī) and the Veda-renunciant (vedasaṃnyāsī); and the householder is of many kinds, distinguished by categories such as the Śālīna and the Yāyāvara," and so forth.

But surely, since in another Smṛti the term *bhikṣu* is mentioned after referring to the *vaikhānasa*, for what purpose is there a different order here? It is said: the difference in order is intended to exclude the *vaikhānasa* from the statement, "The first three [stages] are for those in the stages of life (*āśrama*)."

If it is argued that this is already established by the very prohibition against his entering the village, we say no; for it is possible that seekers might go to the forest as well. And so says another Smṛti:
"The master of the four Vedas, the dialectician, the etymologist, and the reciter of Dharma..."
The celibate student, the householder, and the mendicant—this assembly consists of at least ten members.
Thus it is said.
But some say:
"Having performed the Prajāpatya sacrifice, in which all one's possessions are given as the sacrificial fee,
and having internalized the sacred fires within himself, a Brāhmaṇa may renounce his home."
Relying on this other Smṛti text, some explain that the difference in sequence has the purpose of showing that renunciation (saṃnyāsa) must be undertaken from the state of the householder alone;
the learned Brahmins should investigate whether this has already been established by the preceding Sūtra or not.
Among them, the householder is the source of the others, because they do not produce offspring on their own.
The householder is the cause for all four stages of life (āśramas), because the others— the student (brahmacārin) and so forth— do not produce offspring.
This statement of reason is intended for the sake of the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa).

Since the status of a *brahmacārin* is established simply by the preservation of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), even for one who eats [the prescribed food], the state of having the vital seed drawn upward (*ūrdhvaretas*) is enjoined.
And thus, even in the case of the forest-dweller (*vaikhānasa*) who maintains a wife, the preservation of celibacy must be practiced;
for it is established by the very context that "of them" [refers to those who maintain celibacy].
The mention [of these] is for the purpose of showing that only those born of householders have the right (*adhikāra*) to the Dharma;
and so says Śātātapa:
"Caṇḍālas, those who have fallen from their vows (*pratyavasita*), wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), and ascetics (*tāpasa*)."
Their offspring, once born, one should cause to dwell together with the Caṇḍālas.

Thus, when it is stated that "the householder alone is their source," the word "alone" (eva) already establishes that the others [the other āśramas] are included in the observance of celibacy; however, this specific mention is so that there may be no turning back for them from that state.
If they were to turn back toward the householder's life, then they become outcastes (caṇḍālas). Why? Because of the aforementioned statement of Śātātapa.
In that regard, they become *caṇḍālas*.

Those who have fallen away (*pratyavasita*) and turned back from their vows—namely, wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*), ascetics (*tāpasa*), perpetual celibates (*naiṣṭhika*), and forest-dwellers (*vaikhānasa*)—the offspring born of them, the king should cause to dwell together with *caṇḍālas*, whether in a village or elsewhere; this is the meaning.

Now, as the duties of the stages of life (*āśrama-dharma*) are to be explained in sequence, and since all stages are equal, having first spoken of the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*), he speaks next to explain the duty of the perpetual celibate (*naiṣṭhika*) which follows in order:
In that regard, it has been stated concerning the religious student (brahmacārin): Gautama 3.4.

In this regard, there is an extension (*atideśa*) stating that whatever has been prescribed for the kindling of the sacred fire and so forth according to the procedure for the initiation (*upanayana*) applies to this [naiṣṭhika] as well.

Now, one might ask: how is it known that this applies only to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*) and not to the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*)? It is said: because it has already been stated regarding the temporary student.
Since the householder, the mendicant, and the forest-dweller are to be described [later], this [rule] applies only to the lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika*).
If it is asked, "Then for what purpose is the mention of the *brahmacārin*? it is for the sake of that very person who has performed the vows of the temporary student (*upakurvāṇa*).
This is for the purpose of establishing that the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika) has this same qualification.

Having stated by way of extension that the very vows of the temporary student (upakurvāṇa) must be performed by the lifelong student as well, he now states the specific rule for the latter: "Dependence upon the teacher until the end. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.5)
Dependence upon the teacher—that is, conforming to his mind—must be maintained until death.
Furthermore:
"One should recite [the mantra] with the remainder of the teacher's ritual duties. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.6)
During times other than those spent in service to the guru, one should perform recitation (japa).
In this way, recitation alone becomes his preeminent means for accomplishing dharma.
Since "teacher" (*ācārya*) was the subject under discussion, the mention of "guru" is for the purpose of including the service of one's mother and father as well.
Thus Manu says:
"Service to these three is declared to be the highest austerity."
Without being authorized by them, one should not practice any other dharma.
Thus it is said.
In the absence of the guru, one's conduct [toward him] should be directed toward his offspring.
In the absence of the teacher, service should be rendered to his offspring;

in the absence of the instructor, service should be rendered to his offspring—this is for the purpose of establishing a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*). The mention of "the teacher" (*guru*) is intended to include the offspring of one who belongs to the same caste (*samānajātīya*).
The mention of "offspring" is for the purpose of excluding the wife.
In the absence of these, [the offering should be made] to an elderly fellow student, or into the fire.

In his absence, [the offering is made] to the son of the guru; in his absence, to one who is senior by virtue of knowledge and so forth; in his absence, to a fellow student (sabrahmacārin), that is, one who has practiced the same Vedic course; and in his absence, to the fire.
Service to Agni is meditation upon Agni in the form of light.
Furthermore, as to what the fruit of this stage of life is, he says:
"One who conducts himself thus, having conquered his senses, attains the world of Brahman. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.9)

Thus, acting according to the instruction, one attains the world of Brahmā, the abode of Brahmā, provided that one has conquered the senses. Since the organ of generation (*upasthendriya*) was mentioned in the context of the instruction on guarding celibacy (*brahmacarya*), this [conquest of the senses] should be understood as referring to the objects of the eye and the other [senses].
As Manu says:
That man who, having heard, touched, seen, tasted, or smelled,
neither rejoices nor desponds, should be known as one who has conquered his senses.
Thus, this very [practice] is the primary one even for those who follow; it is for this purpose that its prescription occurs at the conclusion of the fruit.
Now he states the common rule for others as well:
"And this is not in conflict with those that follow" (Gautama Sūtra 3.10).

Whatever has been prescribed for the religious student (brahmacārin) applies to those who follow him as well, provided it is not contradictory—such as the avoidance of gambling and similar activities.

That which is contradictory is excluded; for example, the fire-ritual (agnikārya) is excluded for the renunciant (pravrajita), and residence in the teacher’s house (gurukulavāsa) is excluded for the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa).
The householder’s observance of celibacy (*brahmacarya*).
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that what is about to be stated hereafter is also not in conflict with the preceding rules, such as:
"One should not converse with barbarians, the impure, or the unrighteous," and so forth.
A monk is one who has no accumulation. // Gautama 3.11 //
Now, the duties of the householder, which follow in sequence, ought to be stated;
if it is asked why they are bypassed and instead those of the mendicant are being described, it is replied here: the householder has much that remains to be said.
