In order that certain dharmas being stated might not be in contradiction with those of the predecessors, they are mentioned out of their sequential order.
If it is argued that [the dharma] of the Vaikhānasa should then be mentioned [first], there is no fault, because it was already spoken according to the sequence of its introduction.
Therefore, it is said regarding the monk:
by the word "non-accumulation," the relinquishing of material objects that are subject to increase is meant,
not of permanent objects such as the topknot or the sacred thread.
But is it not the case that the abandonment of only the permanent [sacred thread] is logical? For by the word *upavīta*, a specific manner of wearing (*nyāsa-viśeṣa*) is denoted:
"When the right hand is raised, one is called *upavītī* by the wise."
Thus [it is said].

The sacred thread (*upavīta*) is so called because it is worn according to its true purpose for sacrifice (*yajña*); however, since he lacks the qualification for performing sacrifices, [he does not wear it].
Nor [should one perform it] in a pit, nor in water, nor when attached to clothing, nor at the three *puṣkara* sites.
He for whom there is no dwelling, no seat, and no food—he alone possesses the knowledge of liberation.
Thus, because of the instruction to renounce the water-pot and other such items;
and also in the Jābāla Śruti, it says: "Having cut his nails and having cast off the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*)," regarding the sacrificial thread.
And because of the teaching on renunciation.

It is said in reply: First, regarding what was stated—that there is no entitlement to sacrifice (*yajña*)—the word "sacrifice" (*yāga*) also applies to the worship of the gods and similar acts. And for him, the worship of the gods indeed exists as the worship of the Supreme Self through meditation.
Why? [Because it is said:
"For one who is constant in the forest, whose senses are conquered, and who brings about the satisfaction of the Universal Self..."
For one whose mind has entered into internal reflection and who is equanimous, there is indeed certain non-returning.

Because of this observation in another Smṛti, and because the qualification belongs specifically to the sacrifice to the Self (ātma-yāga), it is likewise heard in the Śruti: "Dharma and Adharma are the oblation; the mind is the sacrificial ladle; the vital breath is the Adhvaryu priest; the senses are the Udgātṛ priests; and sound and the other sense-objects are the Hotṛ priests.
With these officiating priests and with that ladle, one should offer that oblation day after day into the fire of the Supreme Self. Thus it is said.
Therefore, because the qualification for yoga exists, there is no fault. As for what was said— "There is no attachment to the water-pot nor to water"—
even there, the abandonment of attachment itself is intended for the sake of avoiding the diversity [of objects] such as the water-pot.
Not [the case] for the water-pot and so forth. Why? Because in that very same [text], it says: "wearing the sacred thread, with a water-pot in his hand."
Because this will be stated [later];

in that regard, if it is argued that—since the phrase "the most righteous among all stations" refers to the eligibility of all stations (*āśrama*) and thus exists as a general rule—it is nevertheless sublated by a specific rule, we say: no.

If it were intended that all stages of life (*āśrama*) have authority therein, then for the sake of constructing the meaning of the sentence in that context, he would have stated "wearing the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*) and having a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) in hand" using an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) alone—just as he previously said, "The avoidance of backbiting, envy, pride, egoism, dishonesty, self-praise, reviling others, hypocrisy, greed, anger, and delusion is the most righteous duty for all stages of life. Thereafter, however, by means of a negative suffix (*abhāvapratyaya*) and with specific reference [to the student], he says: "wearing the sacred thread and having a water-pot in hand."
Thus, it can be understood that this instruction is intended for the purpose of terminating eligibility for all stages of life (āśrama).

Consequently, since there is no eligibility for any stage of life therein, one can certainly conclude that the mere abandonment of attachment is enjoined by the statement, "There is no attachment to a hut nor to water," so as to avoid the contingency of contradiction between earlier and later passages.
The term *saṅga* (attachment) is used precisely for that purpose.

Therefore, by that [term] as well, there is no renunciation of the wall and so forth. As for what was said—“having clipped the nails, one should discard the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*)”—even there, at the time of first entering the stage of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), one merely performs the discarding of the old sacred thread.
At that time, there is no prohibition regarding what is being taken up.
Why? Because another Smṛti text is heard: "Having pared his nails, and having discarded his old garment, sacred thread, and water-pot, he should take up new ones and enter the stage of life."
Therefore, there is the relinquishing of that substance which is accumulative.
Furthermore, if one were to renounce permanent possessions, it would follow that a monk would lack the means for ritual sipping (ācamana);
since the rule "one should sip water while wearing the sacred thread" (yajñopavītin) is prescribed, in the absence of that [thread], the sipping of water itself would also become impossible.

If it is argued that— just as in the case of the statement "either shaven-headed or with a topknot" (*muṇḍaśikhī vā*), you accept the performance of the *ācamana* even for one who belongs to the shaven-headed group and is thus devoid of the *śikhā* (topknot) which is an ancillary part of the *ācamana*— the same applies to us as well, we say: no.
In that regard, there is no fault because of the scriptural injunction: "He may be shaven-headed or wear a topknot.
However, for you, since there is no such injunction stating that the sacred thread must be discarded, it remains a fault indeed.

Although it should have been stated as "a monk who has no accumulation," the mention of "dharma" at the beginning is for the purpose of including the renunciation of even those things considered eternal, such as the *agnihotra* fire and one's wife.
Thus, he who would go forth from the life of a householder must renounce both the *śrauta* and *smārta* fires, along with the elaborations of wife, sons, sacrifices, and so forth.

For one who would renounce the world from the state of a Vaiśvānara, even in that case where he has reached the stage of being accompanied by a wife, there must be the abandonment of the household fire along with the Śrāmaṇaka fire, as well as the five great sacrifices and so forth.

Some explain that the initial mention [of the lifelong student] is for the purpose of prescribing his lack of accumulation even while he is a *naiṣṭhika*; however, that is incorrect, because of the rule:
"He should mutter [the Veda] with the remainder of his duties toward the teacher."

Since it is taught that the recitation (japa) alone is the primary element, it can be understood that by that very fact, even the ritual acts such as the formal adoption of the sacred fire (agniparigraha) and so forth are absent.
One whose semen is drawn upward. // Gautama 3.12 //

By the statement, "And this is not in conflict with those [rules] for the northerners," since his [the student's] celibacy is already established by the protection of chastity prescribed for the *brahmacārin*, the mention of "one whose semen is drawn up" (*ūrdhvaretas*) is for the purpose of indicating that one should employ whatever means are necessary so that the depletion of semen does not occur.
And the means [for this] is the consumption of little food and so forth.
As the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva has said:
"The objects of the senses turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food."
With the exception of taste; even taste ceases for him upon seeing the Supreme.
Thus, with the intention of referring to the consumption of very little food, it is also stated in another Smṛti: "Eight mouthfuls are the meal of a sage," and so forth.
And in this way, there is no fault in a student (brahmacārin) eating a full meal.
And so another Smṛti states:
"The ox, the student, and the one who has established the sacred fires—these three achieve success only while eating; for them there is no success through fasting."
Thus, one who is firm in his conduct [should remain] during the rainy season. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.13)
Because of the plural form "during the rains," the meaning is that one should not travel from village to village during the four months [of the rainy season].
The mention of "conduct" (*śīla*) is because even if one stays in a single place, there might still be the exertion of wandering;
by this very point, his state of being homeless is established.
And so another Smṛti states: "At the edge of a village, in a temple, in an empty house, or at the root of a tree.
By mentioning the adoption of virtuous conduct (*śīla*), he makes it known that this [specific location] need not necessarily be the case.
And consequently, one may even go [to another land] during times such as famine or the collapse of one's kingdom.
Seeking alms, he should go to the village. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.14)
"Begging" refers to food because it is obtained by begging, as well as clothing, a water-pot, and so forth;
for the sake of these, he should go to the village—it follows, therefore, that at all other times he should remain in the forest, in a temple, or similar places.
When the time for alms-seeking has arrived, the student should say: "I shall go for the lowest [alms], without turning back. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.15)
"Jaghanyam" means after the act of eating;
thus says Manu:
"When the smoke has ceased, when the pestle is laid aside, when the embers are extinguished, and when the people have finished eating..."
Once the exchange of alms-bowls has taken place, the ascetic should always go out for alms.
Thus:

"not returning" means that on the day one has been refused entry at a house, one should not enter that house again on that same day. The word "should act" (*caret*) is used for the purpose of including other Smṛti texts.
As Vasiṣṭha said: "When the smoke has ceased and the pestle lies still, clad in a single garment or in a deerskin."
One whose desire for rewards has ceased. // Gautama 3.16 //
The meaning is that he does not offer blessings in response to alms-giving, salutations, and so forth.
If it is argued that this is already obtained by the phrase "one who does not undertake violence or favoring," we say no.
Because favor has the nature of an action,
and because a blessing has the nature of speech.
One should be restrained in speech, sight, and action. // Gautama 3.17 //

Since this is already established by the statement "restrained in speech, arms, and belly" within the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), this repetition is for the sake of emphasizing excellence;
therefore, restraint of speech is silence (*mauna*).
Except for the recitation of sacred texts, the chanting of mantras, inquiries regarding the path, and inquiries concerning the application of dharma— for these he does not censure even a mendicant:

"The application of dharma, inquiries regarding the path, and likewise the recitation of sacred texts, as well as the words 'give' spoken for the sake of alms— he does not criticize these even in the case of an ascetic."
This is because of the statement in another Smṛti:
"Restraint of the eyes" means that one must not even look at one's own disease.
And so Vasiṣṭha says: "Indifferent toward all beings.
Restraint of action consists merely in the performance of what is prescribed, so that there may be no engagement in actions performed for the sake of desire.
Now, by the statement "a monk is one who has no accumulation," a counter-exception is made regarding the renunciation of all accumulative property:
he may wear a garment for the purpose of covering his private parts. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.18)
"Kaupīna" refers to nakedness;
one should wear only such clothing as serves to cover it.
And thus, there is no fault in accepting just that much from praiseworthy members of the twice-born.
And then: he who, having granted fearlessness to all beings, turns back [from his vow].
He who always accepts [such gifts] destroys both those already born and those yet to be born.
Thus, the enumeration of faults found in another Smṛti should be understood as referring to something other than this [present case].
Some, having washed it, have abandoned it. (Gautama 3.19)

Some think that for the sake of avoiding the fault of accepting [garments], one should wash and then wear what has been discarded on the road or elsewhere; the word "having washed" (*nirṇijya*) is used for the purpose of attaining personal purification.
One should not take a limb from medicinal plants or trees that has not been detached [from the parent body].
Herbs (oṣadhi) are those that perish at the ripening of their fruit.
Those that bear fruit without flowers are forest trees (vanaspati).
By including both categories, all immobile beings (sthāvara) are also encompassed.

If it is argued that this is already established by the rule "one who does not undertake acts of injury or favor" (A 1.31.7), which implies that one should not take branches, leaves, and so forth— which are inseparable from and not distinct from those [trees]— some maintain that in this context, "injury" (hiṃsā) refers exclusively to the killing of mobile beings.
There is no fault, because it was stated with that intention;
furthermore, due to the prefix *upa*, even the instigator would not be [the agent].
Since it has been taught that one's conduct must be constant, and because there might otherwise be the inclination to act according to one's own will outside of the rainy season, he says:
"One may stay in a village for a second night during the non-rainy season. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.21)
By the word *ṛtu*, only the rainy season is meant.
When the rainy season has passed, he should not stay for a second night in a village;
the meaning is that he should not stay in a single village for two days.
By the mention of "village," there is no fault in staying in the forest. By the mention of "non-season," there is no fault even if one stays for a second [period] during the rainy season;
by the word "rainy season" (varṣā), the winter and summer seasons are also implied.
And consequently, it follows as a matter of course that during that rainy season one should reside in one place alone and not elsewhere.
He may be either shaven-headed or wear a topknot.
This undertaking is for the purpose of prohibiting the wearing of matted hair.
There is an option according to one's preference.
One should avoid the destruction of seeds. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.23)
One should not perform the destruction of seeds, such as rice and so forth, by means of threshing and other such methods.
He is equal toward all beings. // Gautama 3.24 //
The meaning is that one should remain impartial toward all living beings, avoiding the distinction between one's own side and the side of others.
He does not engage in either harming or favoring others.
Since this is already established by the word "violence" (*hiṃsām*) in the section on the religious student (*brahmacārin*), this repetition is for the sake of emphasizing the gravity of the matter.

Consequently, even when the killing of a living being is unknown, an expiation must be performed day after day to avoid that [sin]. Thus says Uśanas: "For the sake of purification from an unknown killing, one should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) during the night and three during the day."
By the word *anugraha*, affection (*sneha*) is meant;
the meaning is that one should not even perform that.
Having spoken concerning the mendicant, he now states the dharma of the forest-dweller (vaikhānasa):
"The forest-dweller, subsisting on roots and fruits in the forest, is devoted to austerity. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.26)
The word *vaikhānasa* has its etymological derivation from *sṛta*.
Its meaning is that one living in the forest should be habituated to eating roots and such, and should not eat prepared food.
One whose nature is austerity is one whose habit is the emaciation of the body;
and thus he should eat even roots, fruits, and the like only in small quantities, because another Smṛti text is seen which states: "For the forest-dweller, sixteen [mouthfuls]."
Having established the sacred fire according to the rite of a recluse. // Gautama 3.27 //
The term *śrāmaṇaka* refers to the manual of the Vaikhānasas;
by means of that, having established the sacred fire and taken it up, one should perform the oblation in the evening and in the morning—this is the remainder [of the sense].
He shall not eat food that is vulgar. 3.28.
One should not eat even wild roots and fruits that have been cultivated.
He should worship the gods, the ancestors, humans, spirits, and sages. // Gautama 3.29 //
The five great sacrifices (*pañca mahāyajñāḥ*) of the householder are accomplished by means of village food (*grāmyānna*).
This [section] is commenced so that, because of the prohibition against non-village food (*agrāmyāhāra*), there might not be a cessation of those [sacrifices].
Thus says Manu:
With various pure forest products, or with vegetables, roots, and fruits,
one should perform these very same great sacrifices according to the prescribed rule.
He should be hospitable to all guests, with the exception of those who are prohibited.
The meaning is that as long as he goes to his hermitage, everyone there is indeed his guest;
there is no restriction of caste, such as "for a brāhmaṇa, a non-brāhmaṇa is not a guest," nor is there any restriction of number.
Those prohibited, such as thieves and others, as well as those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), are excluded; with these exceptions.
One may also consume garlic. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.31)
The meat of an animal killed by wild beasts such as tigers is "vaiṣka"; one may consume that. The word "api" (even/also) is used here in a sense of censure.
Thereafter, one should employ it only in times of distress.
He should not stand upon ground that has been ploughed by a plow.
Even in the forest, one should not step upon ground that has been ploughed;
the meaning is that one should not make a dwelling there.

Although "should step upon" (*ākrāmet*) would have sufficed, the use of the term "should occupy" (*adhitiṣṭhet*) is intended to indicate the absence of fault even when one steps upon such ground through inadvertence.
Since the meaning "ploughed" is already established, the inclusion of the word "field" (*phāla*) is for the purpose of prohibiting residence in the vicinity of a field.
And he should not enter a village.
One should not enter a human habitation even by a path not ploughed by a plow;
by the use of the word "and," [it is implied that one should not enter] even another village.
He has matted hair and wears garments of bark and deerskin. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.34)

"Jaṭila" means one with matted hair (*keśin*). This rule is formulated for the purpose of restriction, so that he must indeed be a *jaṭila*. "Cīra" refers to [garments] made from *darbha* grass and the like.
This is to be seen as the lower garment; the *ajina* is the skin;
this is the upper garment.
And so another Smṛti states: "Clad in bark garments and with a deerskin as an upper garment."
One should not eat more than once a year.
One should not consume even roots and fruits that are more than a year old;
likewise, Manu says: "In the month of Āśvayuja, one should discard [old provisions]," and so forth.
And thus...
The accumulation for exactly one year was accomplished.

Having spoken regarding the Vaikhānasa, he now says, desiring to state the position that the stages of life (āśrama) are mutually exclusive according to the opinion of some teachers: "But the teacher [maintains] a single stage of life, because of the direct injunction for the householder's life; [the repetition] 'of the householder' is for emphasis. (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 3.36)
"Aikāśramya" means existing in a single āśrama;
the word "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis.
The genitive case in "gārhasthyasya" is used in the sense of the object (karmaṇi).
The teachers maintain that the householder's life alone is the goal. Why? Because of direct injunction; that is to say, because of the injunction found in the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Even though it is not explicitly enjoined in the form "one should become a householder," [the meaning follows from the context].
Nevertheless, since the performance of rites such as the Agnihotra is prescribed for the householder, it should be understood that the injunction refers specifically to him.
Thus ends the third chapter in the Maskarīya Gautama-bhāṣya.
